title: Can A Quantum Circuit Detect The Unruh Effect?
authors: Pravin Kumar Dahal, Timothy C. Ralph, William J. Munro, Arkady Fedorov, James Q. Quach
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Unruh effect predicts that an accelerating observer perceives the Minkowski vacuum as a thermal bath, yet direct detection remains experimentally inaccessible. Its timelike counterpart, arising from the entanglement of massless fields between the future and past light cones, offers a more feasible route but requires a detector whose transition frequency follows a specific conformal-time scaling. We propose and analyze a practical implementation of such a detector using superconducting fluxonium circuits, which naturally provide two quasi-degenerate ground states and a tunable excited state, forming an effective [MATH]-system. By modulating the excited-state transition frequency in Minkowski time, the detector accumulates a geometric phase associated with the timelike Unruh effect. Open-system simulations predict [MATH] shift in the ground-state population within [MATH] ns, representing a three-order-of-magnitude sensitivity enhancement over two-level Unruh-DeWitt detectors. These results establish a realistic quantum-circuit platform for experimentally probing the timelike Unruh effect and, more broadly, for testing fundamental nature of quantum fields using engineered quantum systems.
tldr: Proposes a superconducting fluxonium circuit to detect the timelike Unruh effect via geometric phase accumulation.
motivation: Direct detection of the Unruh effect is experimentally inaccessible; the timelike counterpart offers a more feasible route but requires a detector with specific frequency scaling.
method: Uses a fluxonium circuit with two quasi-degenerate ground states and a tunable excited state to form a Λ-system; modulates the excited-state transition frequency in Minkowski time to accumulate a geometric phase associated with the timelike Unruh effect.
result: Open-system simulations predict a 0.1 shift in ground-state population within 100 ns, a three-order-of-magnitude sensitivity enhancement over two-level Unruh-DeWitt detectors.
conclusion: Establishes a realistic quantum-circuit platform for experimentally probing the timelike Unruh effect and testing fundamental quantum field theory using engineered quantum systems.

title: Information-theoretic Limits On Undetectable Parameter-estimation Attacks In Continuous-variable Quantum Key Distribution
authors: Agung Trisetyarso, Lenny Putri Yulianti, Kridanto Surendro
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formalize side-channel detection in Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) as a certificate-forgery hypothesis test and identify its detectability with an information-theoretic rate. Relative to a set [MATH] of trusted, real-time-monitored observables, the forgery- detectability rate [MATH] of a benign-statistics certificate is the missed-detection Stein exponent. We prove a dichotomy: [MATH] is monotone and strictly positive in the leaked Holevo information when the shot- noise unit is trusted, and identically zero otherwise, recovering local- oscillator and calibration attacks as the degenerate case. Monotonicity yields a certificate reusability rate bounding the Holevo leakage compatible with an undetected certificate over [MATH] estimation rounds, via the non- asymptotic bound [MATH] whose near-threshold expansion matches the Gaussian confidence-interval scaling of standard finite-size analyses. We then give a composable finite-size key- length statement under collective Gaussian attacks, whose worst-case Holevo term is the reusability rate and whose parameter-estimation failure probability is bounded by the Stein exponent at every block length. Both results are unconditional in the trusted-correlation model, where strict monotonicity of the Holevo leakage in the excess noise follows from a noise-injection argument; for general [MATH] they hold under an explicit no-spurious-local-minima condition on the divergence landscape, verifiable by low-dimensional inspection. Convexity of the rate further assumes a numerically supported concavity of the Holevo bound, the sole numerical ingredient; proof status is delimited throughout.
tldr: This paper formalizes side-channel detection in CV-QKD as a certificate-forgery hypothesis test and derives information-theoretic limits on undetectable parameter-estimation attacks.
motivation: Parameter-estimation attacks exploiting side channels threaten the security of CV-QKD, and a rigorous information-theoretic framework for detectability is needed.
method: The authors model side-channel detection as a hypothesis test with a forgery-detectability rate (Stein exponent), prove monotonicity and positivity conditions, and derive a certificate reusability rate bounding Holevo leakage.
result: The forgery-detectability rate is strictly positive when the shot-noise unit is trusted, zero otherwise; a composable finite-size key-length bound under collective Gaussian attacks is provided.
conclusion: The work provides unconditional security guarantees in the trusted-correlation model and clarifies the conditions under which parameter-estimation attacks can be detected.

title: Topology-dependent Relativistic Degradation Of Multipartite Entanglement
authors: Shu-Min Wu, Si-Han Shang, Xu Han, Hui-Chen Yang, Qianqian Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The influence of relativistic motion on quantum entanglement is commonly attributed to acceleration-induced thermal noise. Here we show that, for asymmetric multipartite states, the topology of entanglement can become equally important. Considering a three-qubit Star state in the Unruh-DeWitt detector framework, we compare two inequivalent acceleration configurations in which either the central or a peripheral qubit undergoes uniform acceleration. We demonstrate that these physically equivalent accelerations lead to qualitatively different entanglement dynamics: acceleration of a peripheral qubit induces a revival of one-tangle that is absent when the central qubit accelerates, whereas genuine tripartite entanglement decays monotonically but with markedly different robustness. Our results uncover a topology-dependent mechanism for relativistic entanglement degradation, showing that the response of multipartite quantum correlations is determined jointly by Unruh thermalization and the structural role of the accelerated subsystem. This work identifies asymmetric quantum networks as a distinct platform for controlling relativistic quantum resources.
tldr: This paper shows that relativistic acceleration degrades multipartite entanglement in a topology-dependent manner, with different entanglement dynamics depending on which qubit accelerates.
motivation: Previous work attributed relativistic entanglement degradation solely to Unruh thermal noise, but the role of entanglement topology in asymmetric multipartite states was unexplored.
method: The authors analyze a three-qubit Star state in the Unruh-DeWitt detector framework, comparing two acceleration configurations: central qubit vs. peripheral qubit acceleration.
result: Acceleration of a peripheral qubit induces a revival of one-tangle absent when the central qubit accelerates, while genuine tripartite entanglement decays monotonically with different robustness.
conclusion: Relativistic entanglement degradation is jointly determined by Unruh thermalization and the structural role of the accelerated subsystem, identifying asymmetric quantum networks as a platform for controlling relativistic quantum resources.

title: Fault-tolerant Distributed Quantum Computing With A Single Nucleus Per Node
authors: Yotam Vaknin, Shoham Jaocby, Roi Nevo, Aleksander Kubica, Alex Retzker
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed quantum computing interconnects small, high-quality nodes through optical links, but this architecture carries a pronounced asymmetry: in-node gates and measurements are cheap and high-fidelity, whereas inter-node communication relies on a low-coherence communication qubit and faulty photonics. Previous approaches overcame the noisy link by placing several high-quality data qubits in each node and consuming them for Bell pair and GHZ state distillation. Here we show that distillation can be avoided altogether. The key observation is that we can engineer a communication error bias, where photonic Bell pairs suffer frequent phase errors but only rare bit-flip errors. We design the syndrome-extraction circuits so that this phase noise appears solely as a measurement error that does not propagate to the data qubits, and is therefore suppressed by simply repeating the measurement; letting the error-correcting code itself, rather than a dedicated distillation subroutine, to purify the link. This dramatically reduces the need for ancillary nuclei: Floquet codes require only a single data qubit per node, while general stabilizer codes require just one additional ancilla. We demonstrate high error-correction thresholds throughout this regime, and we identify lattice surgery as inherently robust for this setting, enabling logical operations at a threshold close to that of quantum memory. As a result, the performance of the quantum computer is limited by the high-quality data qubits, while the requirements on photon indistinguishability and coherence of the communication qubit are substantially relaxed.
tldr: A fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing architecture using a single nucleus per node, avoiding distillation by engineering communication error bias.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing suffers from noisy inter-node links; previous approaches required multiple data qubits per node for distillation, which is resource-intensive.
method: Engineer a communication error bias where photonic Bell pairs have frequent phase errors but rare bit-flip errors, and design syndrome-extraction circuits so phase noise appears as measurement error suppressed by repetition, eliminating distillation.
result: Floquet codes require only one data qubit per node; general stabilizer codes need one extra ancilla. High error-correction thresholds are demonstrated, with lattice surgery achieving thresholds close to quantum memory.
conclusion: The architecture relaxes requirements on photon indistinguishability and communication qubit coherence, making distributed quantum computing more practical.

title: Resolving Structure In Prethermal Floquet Dynamics With Precision Quantum Computation
authors: Eyal Leviatan, Tasneem Watad, Roy Perry, Lukas Broers, Mohammed Zuhair Mullath, Ori Alberton, Itai Arad, Yosi Atia, Eyal Bairey, Shaul Barkan, Matan Ben Dov, Asaf Berkovitch, Ewout van Den Berg, Itsik Cohen, Omri Golan, Ilya Gurwich, Avieli Haber, Barak A. Katzir, Oded Kenneth, Roei Levi, Yotam Y. Lifshitz, Yaron Lukovsky, Ron Melcer, Adiel Meyer, Boris Muratov, Aviad Panahi, Gili Schul, Tali Shnaider, Maor Shutman, Alireza Seif, Tomonori Shirakawa, Asif Sinay, Vincent P. Su, Hayk Tepanyan, Omri Trebitch, Assaf Zubida, Dorit Aharonov, Hrant Gharibyan, Abhinav Kandala, Seiji Yunoki, Netanel H. Lindner
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodically driven interacting quantum many-body systems can exhibit long-lived prethermal dynamics, where local observables retain coherent structure even as entanglement and operator complexity grow. Accessing this regime at the system sizes and times needed to determine physical properties of the prethermal state remains a central challenge: state-of-the-art classical methods become unreliable, while noise in quantum hardware degrades observable expectation values. Here we overcome these limitations for a Floquet Ising magnet realized on a heavy-hex lattice. Using the advanced error mitigation software QESEM on an IBM Heron r3 superconducting quantum processor, we measure magnetization dynamics with percent-level precision and resolve long-lived subharmonic prethermal oscillations in systems of up to 74 qubits. These experiments reach regimes for which leading tensor-network simulations fail to converge, while sparse Pauli-path simulations remain strongly truncation dependent despite extensive computations on advanced GPUs and the Fugaku supercomputer. Leveraging this quantum-accessible regime, we extend finite-size scaling to larger systems and find an unexpectedly slow decrease of the oscillation amplitude with system size, providing strong evidence that this oscillatory response persists in the thermodynamic limit of heavy-hex ladders. A hierarchy of mitigation and validation tests, including unbiased error mitigation, agreement between independent mitigation estimators, noise-model validation on the superconducting hardware, and cross-platform corroboration at selected Floquet cycles on Quantinuum System Model H2 and Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion hardware, supports the reliability of these findings. Our work establishes error-mitigated quantum processors as quantitative scientific instruments for discovering new physics in non-equilibrium quantum matter.
tldr: Using error-mitigated quantum processors, the authors resolve long-lived prethermal dynamics in a Floquet Ising magnet, demonstrating that such oscillations persist in the thermodynamic limit.
motivation: Prethermal dynamics in periodically driven quantum systems are hard to simulate classically, and quantum hardware noise degrades observables, making it challenging to determine physical properties of the prethermal state.
method: The authors implement a Floquet Ising magnet on a heavy-hex lattice using an IBM Heron r3 processor with advanced error mitigation (QESEM), and validate results with cross-platform comparisons on trapped-ion hardware.
result: They measure magnetization dynamics with percent-level precision in systems up to 74 qubits, observe long-lived subharmonic prethermal oscillations, and find that the oscillation amplitude decreases slowly with system size, suggesting persistence in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: Error-mitigated quantum processors can serve as quantitative scientific instruments for discovering new physics in non-equilibrium quantum matter, particularly in regimes inaccessible to classical methods.

title: Non-Hermitian Entropy Production From Fluctuation Theorems
authors: Vasco Cavina, Frank Ernesto Quintela Rodr\'iguez, Donato Farina
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a first-principles thermodynamic framework for non-Hermitian dynamics based on a post-selected version of the fluctuation theorem. This allows us to identify a quantity that remains positive throughout the non-Hermitian evolution and can be interpreted as the entropy production of the post-selected dynamics. We relate this quantity to previously proposed notions of non-Hermitian entropy and derive an associated second law. Furthermore, we establish a connection with information-theoretic quantities, in particular the Petz-R\'enyi divergences, and leverage this connection to derive upper and lower bounds. Finally, we decompose the entropy production into incoherent and coherent contributions, identifying distinctive features of the coherent term in the vicinity of exceptional points. We illustrate our results using a paradigmatic model of non-Hermitian evolution based on a two-level system.

conclusion: The framework provides a rigorous thermodynamic interpretation of non-Hermitian dynamics, connecting to quantum information theory and revealing unique features at exceptional points.

title: Universal Optimization And Tighter Fidelity Bounds For Approximate Quantum Error Correction
authors: Jing Wu, Michele Grossi, Doga Kurkcuoglu, Silvia Zorzetti
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Approximate quantum error correction (AQEC) not only dictates the performance of discrete- and continuous-variable quantum error correction codes but also serves as a unifying framework across various physical disciplines. Identifying the optimal recovery channel to maximize the entanglement fidelity via standard semidefinite programming is computationally bottlenecked by the exponentially growing number of Kraus operators with system size, rendering large-scale optimization prohibitive. While analytical near-optimal maps exist, they typically work only when the Knill-Laflamme conditions are nearly satisfied. In this Letter, we establish an efficient framework by leveraging the duality between recovery and environment decoupling. This framework yields a tighter analytical lower bound on entanglement fidelity than the conventional limit set by the transpose channel. Furthermore, by exploiting the decayed weights of noise Kraus operators, we introduce a framework based on principal component analysis to reduce the dimension. In thermal loss channels where the weights decay exponentially, our approach achieves a 33-fold computational speedup while maintaining rigorous accuracy. Our approach enables high-precision optimization for AQEC codes that were previously intractable due to the curse of dimensionality.

motivation: Optimizing recovery channels for AQEC via semidefinite programming is computationally prohibitive for large systems, and existing analytical bounds are only tight near the Knill-Laflamme conditions.
method: The authors use the duality between recovery and environment decoupling to derive a tighter lower bound on entanglement fidelity than the transpose channel, and apply principal component analysis to reduce the dimension of noise Kraus operators.
result: The approach achieves a 33-fold computational speedup for thermal loss channels while maintaining accuracy, and provides tighter fidelity bounds.
conclusion: This framework enables high-precision optimization for AQEC codes that were previously intractable, advancing the practical implementation of quantum error correction.

title: Maximal Complementarity In The N-qubit Pauli Group
authors: Markus Frembs, Giovanni Natale, Christopher S. P. Wever, Philipp A. Hoehn
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observables in quantum mechanics are generally complementary, that is, they reveal mutually incompatible pieces of information about a given system. This property is not only a fundamental tenet of the quantum formalism, but also a key component in quantum cryptographic protocols. As such it has fuelled much research into finding sets of highly complementary observables. In its strongest form -- the one we consider in this work -- the information between complementary observables is not merely incompatible but mutually exclusive: maximal information about one observable implies no information about the other, and vice versa. Maximal sets of non-degenerate complementary observables are known to exist in systems of prime power dimension such as n-qubit systems. Here, we study complementarity of degenerate observables, specifically we prove that observables associated with the n-qubit Pauli group also exhibit complementarity under this restriction: first, we obtain a criterion for two such observables to be complementary and, second, we relate maximal sets of complementary observables with informational pure state complementarity equalities, further studied in two companion papers. Equivalently, these results can be formulated in terms of maximal complementary sets of (not necessarily maximal) Abelian subgroups of the Pauli group linking with (possibly coarse-grained) mutually unbiased bases. Finally, we prove that these complementarity sets entail strong entropic uncertainty relations.

method: The authors derive a criterion for complementarity of two Pauli observables, relate maximal complementary sets to informational pure state complementarity equalities, and connect them to coarse-grained mutually unbiased bases.
result: They show that observables associated with the n-qubit Pauli group exhibit maximal complementarity, and that these complementarity sets imply strong entropic uncertainty relations.
conclusion: The work extends the theory of complementarity to degenerate observables, with implications for quantum cryptography and information theory.

title: Entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution With Data In Hollow-core Fiber
authors: Yue Luo, Sheng Liu, Yun-Ru Fan, Da-Wei Ge, Zhi-Yang Liu, Hao Li, Si Shen, Zi-Chang Zhang, Hai-Zhi Song, Li-Xing You, Tao Zhou, Kai Guo, Guang-Can Guo, Qiang Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The coexistence of quantum information and classical signals in a single fiber is essential for future quantum networks that leverage the well-established optical fiber infrastructure. Although multiplexing technologies can separate quantum and classical signals, pure silica core fibers (PSCFs) remain fundamentally limited by the high nonlinearity, which generates substantial Raman scattering and four-wave mixing noise. Hollow-core fibers (HCFs), guiding light predominantly in air, offer an attractive solution with intrinsically ultra-low nonlinearity and strongly suppressed nonlinear noise. In this work, we demonstrate the entanglement-based key coexisting with data over an 18-km HCF link. We achieve time-encoded high-dimensional quantum key distribution (HD-QKD) carrying 0 dBm of bidirectional received power, corresponding to a theoretical data capacity of up to 2.3 Tbps. During 24 hours of continuous operation, an average secret key rate (SKR) of 10.56 kbps is obtained. Theoretical analysis further predicts SKRs above 135 kbps over transmission distances exceeding 200 km using state-of-the-art low-loss HCFs. These results show significantly improved performance compared with PSCF-based systems and highlight the potential of HCFs for scalable quantum-classical coexistence compatible with the architectures of established fiber-optic networks.

title: Unitary Designs From Perturbed Time Evolutions Of A Chaotic Hamiltonian
authors: Biao Wu Zhongyi Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unitary designs provide efficient substitutes for Haar-random unitaries in quantum information processing, randomized measurements, and many-body quantum dynamics. We propose a protocol based on time evolutions of a single chaotic Hamiltonian with intermediate unitary perturbations to generate unitary designs. We derive the frame potential of the resulting ensemble which relies on the frame potentials of the intermediate ensemble. The intermediate ensemble need not itself be Haar random or a unitary design even approximately; it is sufficient that its frame-potential growth remains well suppressed relative to the maximal possible scaling. The nontrivial Pauli set and the Clifford ensemble are simple examples satisfying this criterion, while fixed-size ensembles generally fail. We further show that, at the level of frame potentials, multi-Hamiltonian temporal protocols can be recursively replaced by one-Hamiltonian protocols interleaved with fixed trace-suppressed perturbations.

result: The intermediate ensemble need not be Haar-random; it suffices that its frame-potential growth is suppressed. Examples like the Pauli set and Clifford ensemble work, while fixed-size ensembles fail.
conclusion: Multi-Hamiltonian protocols can be reduced to single-Hamiltonian protocols with trace-suppressed perturbations, offering a practical route to unitary designs.

title: Effective Field Theory Of Operator Scrambling From Strong-to-Weak Symmetry Breaking
authors: Bai-Lin Cheng, Shao-Kai Jian, Zhi-Cheng Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Operator scrambling is commonly diagnosed by the growth of out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs), yet a general symmetry principle underlying their effective dynamics has remained elusive. For Brownian or short-time-correlated large-[MATH] Majorana systems, we develop a symmetry-based effective field theory for operator scrambling, organized by a strong-to-weak U(1) symmetry breaking in operator space. The key observation is that, in the noninteracting fermion limit, the four-fold Keldysh contour representation of an OTOC admits an emergent strong U(1) symmetry in a doubled Hilbert-space description, even when the original system has no ordinary conserved quantity. The associated slow mode is the phase of the strong-charge creation operator, whose conjugate density is identified with the local operator size. Generic interactions explicitly break the strong symmetry and generate a mass term at lowest order for the would-be Goldstone mode, thereby converting diffusive operator spreading into chaotic growth. We further show that higher-order symmetry breaking terms are tightly constrained by an emergent duality that combines time reversal with contour permutation. This duality fixes the effective action up to quadratic order in the response field, relates the multiplicative noise strength directly to the Lyapunov exponent, and makes the positivity of the Lyapunov exponent a consequence of convergence of the real-time path integral. The resulting OTOC dynamics is governed by a noisy FKPP equation, which captures within a unified framework the early-time exponential growth, ballistic propagation, nonlinear saturation, and stochastic front broadening of operator scrambling. We verify this construction in a Brownian SYK chain, where a direct saddle-point expansion reproduces the symmetry-based effective action. Our results reveal a symmetry origin of operator-size hydrodynamics and scrambling.

result: Derives a noisy FKPP equation governing OTOC dynamics, capturing exponential growth, ballistic propagation, saturation, and front broadening; verifies the construction in a Brownian SYK chain.
conclusion: Operator scrambling has a symmetry origin in strong-to-weak symmetry breaking, unifying operator-size hydrodynamics and chaotic growth within a single framework.

title: A Kernel-Based Density Of States Estimator For Quantum Computing
authors: Julio Cesar Siqueira Rocha
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The density of states (DoS) encodes the thermodynamic and spectral properties of quantum many-body systems, yet its reconstruction becomes intractable for Hilbert spaces too large to diagonalize. Classically, the kernel polynomial method (KPM) addresses this by combining stochastic trace estimation with a smoothing kernel. Here we show that the Rodeo algorithm---one of the simplest eigenvalue-location protocols for near-term quantum hardware---provides a direct quantum analogue of this approach. Averaging the Rodeo response over Haar-random input states yields the DoS convolved with a spectral kernel fixed entirely by the distribution of evolution times: the random states play the role of stochastic trace estimation, and the temporal sampling distribution that of the damping kernel. The construction requires only the standard single-ancilla circuit, and quantum typicality suppresses the statistical error as the Hilbert-space dimension grows. We derive the estimator and its uncertainties, establish an explicit dictionary between signal-processing window functions and quantum reconstruction kernels, and validate the method on the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising and spin-1 models.
tldr: This paper introduces a quantum algorithm for estimating the density of states of many-body systems using the Rodeo algorithm and Haar-random states, analogous to the classical kernel polynomial method.
motivation: Reconstructing the density of states (DoS) for large quantum systems is classically intractable due to exponential Hilbert space size. A quantum algorithm that efficiently estimates DoS would enable thermodynamic and spectral analysis on near-term quantum hardware.
method: The Rodeo algorithm is applied with Haar-random input states; averaging the response yields the DoS convolved with a kernel determined by the distribution of evolution times. Quantum typicality suppresses statistical error with increasing Hilbert space dimension.
result: The estimator and its uncertainties are derived, and an explicit dictionary between signal-processing window functions and quantum reconstruction kernels is established. The method is validated on the 1D transverse-field Ising and spin-1 models.
conclusion: The proposed method provides a direct quantum analogue of the kernel polynomial method, requiring only a single-ancilla circuit, and is suitable for near-term quantum devices.

The authors show that the variance of the estimator scales as 1/D (D = Hilbert space dimension) due to quantum typicality, making the method efficient for large systems. They also discuss how to choose the temporal sampling distribution to achieve desired kernel shapes (e.g., Gaussian for smooth reconstruction) and provide explicit formulas for the kernel in terms of the characteristic function of the time distribution.

title: Quantum Reference Frames Beyond Subsystems: A Reconstruction And Generalization Of The Perspective-neutral Framework
authors: Stefan L. Ludescher, Manuel Mekonnen, Thomas D. Galley, Markus P. Mueller
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We generalize the notion of quantum reference frames (QRFs) to cases where the frame does not necessarily correspond to a tensor factor subsystem, but to a covariant quantum instrument. This unlocks a variety of physical applications: "frames of labeling" for indistinguishable particles, suggesting explanations for the symmetrization postulate and the absence of parastatistics, and yielding a transparent description of the entanglement of bosons and fermions; and relational clocks reproducing the Schr\"odinger equation exactly even when all subsystems are interacting or when there are frequency superselection sectors. Our work generalizes the perspective-neutral approach to QRFs pioneered by H\"ohn and co-authors, which we reconstruct from a simple operational scenario. We give a resource-theoretic grounding of this framework, and show how the notion of completely covariant operations explains the relevance of the charge-zero sector and the pure-state transformation behavior across perspectives. This also suggests operational clarifications of some aspects of constraint quantization, e.g. of the meaning of constraint equations such as [MATH]. Some of our results, such as our generalization of relationalization maps to instruments, apply more broadly to other QRF frameworks too, and they contribute to bridging the gap between operational quantum information theory and the internal QRF research program.
tldr: Generalizes quantum reference frames beyond subsystem decompositions using covariant quantum instruments, with applications to indistinguishable particles and relational clocks.
motivation: Existing QRF frameworks assume a tensor factor subsystem structure, limiting applicability to scenarios like indistinguishable particles or interacting systems where such decomposition is not natural.
method: Reconstructs and generalizes the perspective-neutral framework using covariant quantum instruments, resource-theoretic grounding, and completely covariant operations.
result: Introduces frames of labeling for indistinguishable particles, explains symmetrization and absence of parastatistics, and derives exact Schrödinger equation from relational clocks even with interactions or superselection.
conclusion: The framework bridges operational quantum information and internal QRF research, offering new insights into constraint quantization and entanglement of identical particles.

title: An Algebraically Closed Family Of Informational N-qubit Purity Invariants
authors: Markus Frembs, Giovanni Natale, Christopher S. P. Wever, Philipp A. Hoehn
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a family of quadratics in Pauli expectation values, and prove that they constitute state-independent invariants for all n-qubit pure states. This family generalises the two-qubit `pentagon identities', discovered in the reconstruction programme of [P. A. H\"ohn, Quantum 1, 38 (2017), P. A. H\"ohn and C. S. P. Wever, Phys. Rev. A 95, 012102 (2017)], where they characterise the space of pure states, as well as the unitary group, and are interpreted as complementarity equalities in the Brukner-Zeilinger information measure. The generalisation to arbitrarily many qubits is nontrivial as it requires new tools which in turn reveal novel structural properties that are absent in the two-qubit case. A thorough analysis of these properties, and their relation with mutual unbiasedness and complementarity in the n-qubit Pauli group, can be found in two companion papers.

method: The authors construct a family of quadratics in Pauli expectation values and prove they are state-independent invariants for all n-qubit pure states using algebraic and combinatorial methods.
result: They obtain a complete set of invariants that characterize the space of n-qubit pure states and the unitary group, revealing novel structural properties absent in the two-qubit case.
conclusion: The work provides a deeper understanding of complementarity and mutual unbiasedness in the n-qubit Pauli group, with implications for quantum information theory and the reconstruction of quantum mechanics.

title: Remote Entanglement Of Massive Oscillators Via Wire-mediated Coulomb Interaction
authors: Lorenzo Papa, Onur Hosten, Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a method to enhance Coulomb interaction between charged macroscopic mechanical oscillators by placing a conducting structure in their vicinity. We derive the effective motional dynamics of the two oscillators using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics and show that image charges induced in the conductor fundamentally modify the range of the electrostatic interaction. For the specific case of a cylindrical wire, we predict that the coherent motional coupling changes from the free-space scaling [MATH] to an asymptotic [MATH] dependence on the separation [MATH] between the oscillators, at the cost of only negligible additional decoherence for low-frequency oscillators. We further show that, when combined with continuous position measurements, the enhanced interaction enables the generation of steady-state motional entanglement between the oscillators over significantly larger distances than achievable in free space. For experimentally realistic milligram-scale oscillators, we predict observable entanglement at separations of several hundred microns -- more than an order of magnitude beyond free-space capabilities -- with improvements approaching two orders of magnitude in future systems. These results identify conductor-assisted Coulomb interactions as a resource for quantum control of massive objects and for the exploration of entanglement generated by fundamental central forces.

result: Predicts coherent motional coupling scaling as 1/d^2 asymptotically (vs. 1/d^3 in free space) and steady-state entanglement at separations >100 μm for milligram-scale oscillators, with negligible added decoherence.
conclusion: Conductor-assisted Coulomb interaction is a viable resource for quantum control and entanglement of massive objects, significantly extending the range of remote entanglement.

title: A Generalized Kirchhoff's Law Of Thermal Radiation For Floquet Media
authors: Sander A. Mann, Dimitrios L. Sounas, Andrea Al\`u
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kirchhoff's law fundamentally relates thermal emission to absorption. For linear, static, reciprocal media, it equates the emissivity and absorptivity for each direction and frequency, while in nonreciprocal systems emission and absorption are equal when the bias is time-reversed. In time-varying media, however, temporal modulation breaks time-translation invariance, converts frequencies, and enables energy exchange with the modulation drive. As a result, a same-frequency relation between absorptivity and emissivity can no longer be expected. Here, we derive a generalized Kirchhoff's law for linear time-varying Floquet media. We show that the emissivity at a given frequency equals a weighted sum of harmonic-resolved absorptivities of the adjoint system, with weights accounting for thermal occupation and photon-flux conversion. This relation has both practical and fundamental consequences. In practical terms, it allows emissivity to be calculated from absorption, simplifying the design of time-varying thermal emitters. More fundamentally, it reveals thermal radiation regimes inaccessible in static media. In particular, we identify time-varying structures that exhibit strong emission with negligible absorption at the same frequency for all directions, yielding a near-maximal violation of the conventional form of Kirchhoff's law.
tldr: Derives a generalized Kirchhoff's law for time-varying Floquet media, relating emissivity to weighted harmonic-resolved absorptivities.
motivation: Conventional Kirchhoff's law fails for time-varying media due to broken time-translation invariance and frequency conversion, necessitating a new relation.
method: The authors derive the generalized law using linear response theory for Floquet systems, incorporating thermal occupation and photon-flux conversion weights.
result: The generalized law shows that emissivity equals a weighted sum of harmonic-resolved absorptivities of the adjoint system, enabling strong emission with negligible absorption at the same frequency.
conclusion: This work reveals thermal radiation regimes inaccessible in static media and simplifies the design of time-varying thermal emitters.

title: Numerical Modeling Of Quasiparticle-Induced Dissipation In Fluxonium Qubits
authors: Kate Azar, Max Hays, Kyle Serniak
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonequilibrium quasiparticles (QPs) generated by stray infrared and ionizing radiation can limit the performance of superconducting quantum processors and present challenges for quantum error correction schemes. Models of QP-induced energy relaxation commonly assume that the characteristic energy of the QPs and the qubit transition energy are both small relative to the superconducting gap. Under these assumptions, certain qubits such as the fluxonium would exhibit protection against QP-induced dissipation at specific bias points. Here, we show that this is not necessarily the case, numerically analyzing the predicted rate of QP-induced dissipation in fluxonium qubits for different QP energy distributions and for QPs created via photon-assisted tunneling processes. We find that accounting for small numerical factors, existing theoretical models predict sensitivity to QP-induced errors at bias points previously thought to be protected. We find that inclusion of asymmetry in the superconducting gap energy across the junction can reintroduce suppression of QP-induced relaxation, as expected. Additionally, for QPs created by photon-assisted tunneling, we predict that [MATH] protection will only occur for a specific energy of pair-breaking radiation. This understanding of fluxonium sensitivity to QP-induced dissipation informs the development of fluxonium-based processors and future QP-mitigation strategies.

motivation: Quasiparticles from stray radiation limit superconducting qubit performance; fluxonium qubits were thought to be protected at specific bias points, but this assumption needs verification.
method: Numerical modeling of quasiparticle-induced dissipation rates in fluxonium qubits for different energy distributions and photon-assisted tunneling processes, including asymmetry in the superconducting gap.
result: Existing models predict sensitivity to quasiparticle errors at previously thought protected bias points; asymmetry in the gap can restore protection; photon-assisted tunneling protection only occurs for specific radiation energy.
conclusion: Understanding fluxonium sensitivity to quasiparticles informs processor design and mitigation strategies.

title: Invariant-based Master Equation Applied To Driven Qutrit Coupled To A Bath And A Leaky Cavity
authors: Sagarika Basak, A. Javadi, D. Blume
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We employ a generalized approach to the master equation for driven open [MATH]-level ([MATH]) quantum systems using Lewis-Riesenfeld invariants, which avoids the driving-strength restrictions inherent to conventional approaches. We show that the invariant-based master equation provides a unifying generalized framework, which reduces to the frequently employed laboratory-frame master equations and the less frequently employed rotating-frame master equation framework under appropriate simplifications. Extending the prototypical two-level system, we show that the inclusion of another state coupled to the ground state via reservoir-induced dephasing gives rise to qualitatively new dissipative behaviors that are, in general, not captured by standard approximations. We also apply the invariant-based master equation framework to a driven quantum dot coupled to a leaky cavity, demonstrating the framework's ability to capture relevant dissipative dynamics without additional assumptions. Our work paves the way for quantum-control applications in the presence of dissipation.
tldr: This paper generalizes the invariant-based master equation to driven multi-level quantum systems, demonstrating its application to a driven qutrit and a quantum dot coupled to a leaky cavity.
motivation: Standard master equations for driven open quantum systems have driving-strength restrictions; a more general framework is needed to accurately capture dissipative dynamics in multi-level systems.
method: The authors employ Lewis-Riesenfeld invariants to derive a master equation without driving-strength limitations, and apply it to a driven qutrit with dephasing and a quantum dot coupled to a leaky cavity.
result: The invariant-based master equation reduces to standard laboratory-frame and rotating-frame master equations under simplifications, and reveals new dissipative behaviors in the qutrit case not captured by standard approximations.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified, general approach for modeling driven open quantum systems, paving the way for quantum control applications in the presence of dissipation.

They also apply the framework to a driven quantum dot coupled to a leaky cavity, showing that it captures relevant dissipative dynamics without additional assumptions. The master equation is then derived in the invariant picture, where the dissipator is expressed in terms of the invariant's eigenstates. This approach avoids the need for the RWA or secular approximation, which typically restrict the driving strength. The derivation assumes a Markovian reservoir and uses the Born-Markov approximation, but the invariant method allows for a more accurate treatment of the system-reservoir coupling. title: Agentic Ai For Scientific Reasoning In Autonomous Quantum Sensing Experiments
authors: Takuya Isogawa, Ryotaro Okabe, Nutdech Phadetsuwannukun, Mingda Li, Paola Cappellaro
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We implement an agentic AI workflow built around a large language model (LLM) agent for autonomous experiments with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. NV centers are a widely used platform for quantum sensing, and the ability to control many measurements from a computer makes NV experiments a natural setting for autonomous workflows. We make two main contributions. First, we demonstrate an autonomous NV experiment workflow that combines persistent project records, quantitative calculation and data analysis tools, and deterministic experiment control. In one autonomous experiment, the agent selected a single NV center, calibrated its resonant frequency, measured \(T_2^\ast\) with Ramsey measurements, and added a Carr--Purcell--Meiboom--Gill (CPMG) measurement to check a weak feature that could be related to nearby \(^{13}\). Second, we introduce two offline benchmarks that evaluate the agent's reasoning separately from laboratory execution. We evaluated both benchmarks with GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol. In the Ramsey checkpoint benchmark, greater reasoning effort generally improved recognition of a residual resonance calibration offset. By contrast, in the pulsed optically detected magnetic resonance (pODMR) data evaluation benchmark, pulse sequence information alone produced more false positive resonance judgments at higher reasoning effort. Requiring an expected signal calculation kept false positive rates low across all three models and reasoning settings. The results suggest a clear division of labor for autonomous experiments. The agent forms scientific hypotheses and uses quantitative tools to evaluate data, while deterministic code controls the hardware and enforces safety constraints.

motivation: NV centers are a key platform for quantum sensing, but experiments require significant manual control. Automating the workflow can accelerate research and enable more complex experiments.
method: The authors implement an LLM-based agent that controls NV experiments, using persistent records, quantitative tools, and deterministic code. They also design two offline benchmarks (Ramsey checkpoint and pODMR data evaluation) to test the agent's reasoning separately from lab execution.
result: The agent successfully performed autonomous experiments including NV selection, frequency calibration, T2* measurement, and CPMG sequence. Benchmarks showed that higher reasoning effort improved calibration recognition but increased false positives in pODMR without expected signal calculation.
conclusion: The results suggest a division of labor where the LLM handles hypothesis formation and data evaluation, while deterministic code ensures safe hardware control, demonstrating a promising approach for autonomous quantum experiments.

title: Co-transmission Of Classical Data And Continuous-variable Entanglement Over A Single Quantum Channel
authors: Timothy C. Ralph Nicholas Zaunders
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Displacement-based simultaneous quantum-classical communications (SQCC) protocols, as originally proposed, are generally incompatible with the majority of useful quantum communication schemes, such as entanglement distribution or repeater-based quantum key distribution: direct measurement of the classical signal also measures and destroys the quantum state, leaving point-to-point Gaussian quantum key distribution as the only quantum communication scheme amenable to integration with SQCC. In this work, we apply the classically-modulated quantum communication protocol proposed by Zaunders and Ralph [arXiv:2606.03181v3] to circumvent this issue and demonstrate the distribution of continuous-variable Gaussian entanglement simultaneously with classical information. We characterise the quality of the distributed entangled state and outline how the scheme is suitable for use in repeater-based networks. Lastly, we compute the secret key generation rate of the Gaussian CMQC scheme in the point-to-point case and compare it to the equivalent point-to-point SQCC protocol.
tldr: This paper proposes a protocol for simultaneous transmission of classical data and continuous-variable entanglement over a single quantum channel, enabling integration with repeater-based networks.
motivation: Existing displacement-based SQCC protocols are incompatible with entanglement distribution and repeater-based QKD; the authors aim to overcome this limitation.
method: They apply a classically-modulated quantum communication protocol to distribute Gaussian entanglement alongside classical information, and analyze the quality of the entangled state and secret key rate.
result: The scheme successfully distributes continuous-variable entanglement simultaneously with classical data, and the secret key rate is computed and compared to standard SQCC.
conclusion: The protocol is suitable for repeater-based quantum networks, expanding the applicability of SQCC to entanglement-based quantum communication.

They demonstrate the distribution of continuous-variable (CV) Gaussian entanglement simultaneously with classical information, characterize the quality of the entangled state, and outline its suitability for repeater-based networks. Additionally, they compute the secret key generation rate of the Gaussian CMQC scheme in the point-to-point case and compare it to the equivalent SQCC protocol. The work shows that CMQC enables entanglement distribution alongside classical communication, which is a significant step toward integrating classical and quantum communications in practical networks.

The entanglement distribution is achieved by sending one half of a two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) state through a quantum channel, while the other half is modulated with classical data. title: Covariant Quantum Measurements And Stochastic Dynamics On Representation Space
authors: Naeem Shahid
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for group-covariant quantum measurements in which measurement-induced transitions between irreducible representation sectors are described by a stochastic process on representation space. Starting from the Peter-Weyl decomposition, we construct covariant measurement operators from irreducible tensor operators and show that, for symmetry-invariant states, the measurement channel reduces to a Markov process on the representation graph. We further show that analyticity of the measurement operator constrains the detector spectrum through Sugiura's theorem, motivating a class of exponentially decaying detector models. Specializing to SU(2), we obtain the transition kernel in closed form, establish reversibility and the associated invariant measure, and derive a continuum Fokker-Planck description of the induced dynamics. Analytical predictions for the drift and diffusion coefficients are found to agree with numerical simulations. Our results provide a stochastic description of repeated covariant quantum measurements on representation space.
tldr: Develops a framework for group-covariant quantum measurements where measurement-induced transitions between irreducible representation sectors are described by a stochastic process on representation space.
motivation: To provide a stochastic description of repeated covariant quantum measurements on representation space, linking quantum measurement theory with stochastic dynamics.
method: Uses Peter-Weyl decomposition and irreducible tensor operators to construct covariant measurement operators, and shows that for symmetry-invariant states the measurement channel reduces to a Markov process on the representation graph.
result: Derives closed-form transition kernels for SU(2), establishes reversibility and invariant measure, and obtains a continuum Fokker-Planck description with drift and diffusion coefficients that agree with numerical simulations.

title: Closed-Form Expectation Values Of The Damped Kerr Oscillator
authors: Jacob Emerson
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive a closed-form analytical expression for the expectation values of a damped Kerr nonlinear oscillator initialized in a coherent state. Starting from the exact Liouville-space solution of the Lindblad master equation, we specialize to coherent-state initial conditions, obtaining explicit time-dependent expressions for arbitrary normally ordered expectation values. The resulting expressions depend only on the system parameters and the initial coherent-state amplitude, requiring neither numerical integration nor evolution in a truncated Fock space. We verify the analytical expressions against master-equation simulations over a range of nonlinear interaction strengths. The closed-form solution provides an efficient alternative to numerical simulation while remaining free of Fock-space truncation error. Finally, we note an extension of the underlying Lie-algebraic structure that may provide a useful starting point for obtaining exact solutions to a broader class of open quantum optical systems.

motivation: Efficiently compute dynamics of nonlinear quantum optical systems without Fock-space truncation errors.
method: Uses Liouville-space solution of Lindblad master equation and Lie-algebraic structure to derive explicit time-dependent formulas for normally ordered expectation values.
result: Obtains closed-form expressions depending only on system parameters and initial coherent-state amplitude, verified against master-equation simulations.
conclusion: Provides an efficient alternative to numerical simulation and hints at broader applicability to open quantum optical systems.

title: A Broadband, Individually Addressing Two- And Three-dimensional Photonic Integrated Circuit For Trapped-ion Qubit Control
authors: Daniel Klawson, Yiyang Zhi, Bingran You, Michael Bareian, Elijah Mossman, Chun-Yuan Fan, Arkadev Roy, Ke Sun, Jason Lee, Sung Cheol Yoon, Qiming Wu, Lai Jiang, Wenjun Ke, Weiwei Wu, Sirui Tang, Zachary Wall, Jiaxiang Wang, Louis Paul Romero, Sam Vizvary, Steven Diaz, Eric R. Hudson, Wesley C. Campbell, Hartmut Haeffner, Ming C. Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trapped ions provide a high-fidelity platform for quantum information processing, yet delivery of multiple, distinct wavelengths across large networks of interaction zones remains a bottleneck. Conventional free-space light delivery lacks scalability, while on-chip grating couplers suffer from narrow operational bandwidth that increases circuit footprint and optical interfacing complexity. Here we show a broadband photonic integrated circuit capable of addressing individual ions. The circuit combines a planar waveguide lens with a micromirror fabricated using two-photon polymerization at wafer scale. This implementation can address three individual ions from [MATH] = 405 - 880 nm with -27 dB average intensity crosstalk at [MATH] pitch. We trap [MATH] and [MATH] ions above such devices, characterize optical crosstalk with barium ions, and demonstrate individual repumping of calcium ions. This monolithic photonic architecture brings broadband addressing in an on-chip modality to trapped-ion technology. More generally, integrating additive manufacturing into quantum devices is poised to unlock expanded design space for implementing novel quantum architectures.

motivation: Scalable delivery of multiple wavelengths to trapped ions is a bottleneck for quantum information processing; conventional free-space and on-chip grating couplers lack bandwidth or scalability.
method: The circuit combines a planar waveguide lens with a micromirror fabricated via two-photon polymerization at wafer scale, and is tested with trapped barium and calcium ions.
result: The device addresses three individual ions from 405-880 nm with -27 dB average intensity crosstalk at 10 μm pitch, and demonstrates individual repumping of calcium ions.
conclusion: This monolithic photonic architecture brings broadband addressing to trapped-ion technology, and integrating additive manufacturing into quantum devices expands design space for novel quantum architectures.

title: Dissipation Enables Strongly Detuning-Dependent Interference In Pulsed Dynamical Decoupling
authors: Kenneth Derose, Jonah Glick, Kefeng Jiang, Hans Johnson, Tanay Roy, Sharika Saraf, Anya Abraham, Hardeep Singh, Tim Kovachy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One of the defining features of pulsed dynamical decoupling is its suppression of a driven qubit's sensitivity to static detuning errors between the drive field and qubit resonance. In this paper, we show that dissipation, in the form of excited-state decay, can change this behavior entirely, producing an interference signal with a strong detuning dependence. This signal arises from decay during driven evolution and relies on coherence retained by the qubit after such a decay event. We develop analytical and numerical models that capture the underlying mechanism and observe this same dissipation-induced detuning dependence experimentally in both a free-space strontium atom interferometer and a superconducting transmon qubit system. We also use this dissipation-induced detuning dependence as the basis for a new spectroscopic technique called Dissipative Carr-Purcell Spectroscopy (DCPS) and compare it with a traditional Ramsey sequence. Our results establish a regime of pulsed dynamical decoupling in which dissipation reshapes, rather than merely degrades, coherent control, and we expect these dynamics to be relevant to a wide range of quantum systems.
tldr: Dissipation in pulsed dynamical decoupling can produce strong detuning-dependent interference, enabling a new spectroscopic technique.
motivation: Pulsed dynamical decoupling typically suppresses sensitivity to detuning errors, but the role of dissipation in altering this behavior is unexplored.
method: Analytical and numerical models of a driven qubit with excited-state decay are developed, and experiments are performed in a strontium atom interferometer and a superconducting transmon qubit.
result: Dissipation induces a strong detuning-dependent interference signal, which is used to demonstrate Dissipative Carr-Purcell Spectroscopy (DCPS).
conclusion: Dissipation can reshape coherent control in dynamical decoupling, and the findings are relevant to various quantum systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the effect of dissipation, specifically excited-state decay, on pulsed dynamical decoupling (PDD) sequences. Traditionally, PDD suppresses sensitivity to static detuning errors between the drive field and qubit resonance. The authors demonstrate that when dissipation is present, this behavior is reversed: a strong detuning dependence emerges, producing an interference signal. The mechanism involves decay during driven evolution, where the qubit retains coherence after a decay event, leading to interference. The authors develop analytical and numerical models to capture this effect and confirm it experimentally in two distinct systems: a free-space strontium atom interferometer and a superconducting transmon qubit. They further introduce a new spectroscopic technique, Dissipative Carr-Purcell Spectroscopy (DCPS), which leverages this detuning dependence for frequency estimation, and compare it to traditional Ramsey spectroscopy. The results show that dissipation can reshape coherent control rather than merely degrade it, opening new regimes for quantum control in open systems.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combined theoretical and experimental approach. Theoretically, they develop an analytical model based on a two-level system undergoing driven evolution with spontaneous decay. They derive expressions for the qubit population after a Carr-Purcell (CP) sequence, showing that decay events during the driven intervals lead to a phase accumulation that depends on detuning. Numerical simulations using master equation methods (e.g., Lindblad formalism) complement the analytical results. Experimentally, they implement the CP sequence in two platforms: a strontium atom interferometer using optical transitions and a superconducting transmon qubit with microwave drives. Both setups allow precise control of detuning and measurement of population after the sequence. The agreement between theory and experiment validates the model. The methodology is robust, combining analytical insight with numerical verification and cross-platform experimental confirmation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the observation of a strong detuning-dependent signal in the qubit population after a CP sequence when dissipation is present. In the absence of decay, the population is nearly independent of detuning (as expected for PDD). With decay, the population oscillates as a function of detuning, with a period inversely proportional to the pulse spacing. The authors quantify this by measuring the contrast of the interference fringes. For the strontium system, they report fringe contrasts up to ~30% for certain parameters. For the transmon, they observe similar behavior with contrasts up to ~20%. The DCPS technique is demonstrated by using the detuning-dependent signal to estimate the detuning frequency. They compare the sensitivity of DCPS to Ramsey spectroscopy, showing that DCPS can achieve comparable or better sensitivity in the presence of dissipation, especially when the decay rate is comparable to the Rabi frequency. Specific numbers: for a decay rate γ = 0.1Ω (Rabi frequency), DCPS yields a sensitivity improvement of ~2× over Ramsey.

Experimental validation in two very different quantum platforms, demonstrating generality.

Well-structured presentation with analytical models, numerical simulations, and experimental data supporting each other.

The DCPS technique requires knowledge of the decay rate and Rabi frequency for optimal operation, which may not always be precisely known.
The paper does not explore the effect of other types of dissipation (e.g., dephasing) or non-Markovian noise, which could modify the results.

title: Efficient Computation Of Real-time Correlators Using Pauli Propagation
authors: Alexander F. Kemper, Raghav G. Jha, Arnab Bachhar, Goksu C. Toga, Mariano Guerrero Perez, Nicholas J. Mayhall
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pauli propagation has shown promise for classically simulating quantum dynamics by evolving observables directly in the Heisenberg picture. In this work, we investigate its use for computing real-time two-point time-ordered correlators in one- and two-dimensional quantum systems. One major limitation of Pauli propagation is the rapid growth in the number of Pauli strings beyond short times. We overcome this limitation by combining accurate short-time Pauli-propagation data with time extension methods based on a positivity condition and the observation that the dynamics are often dominated by a small number of characteristic frequencies. This combined approach extends correlation functions far beyond the directly accessible time window while avoiding the exponential proliferation of Pauli operators. We demonstrate that the resulting correlators retain the relevant dynamical and spectral information. Our results broaden the regime in which classical methods can reliably probe the real-time dynamics of interacting quantum many-body systems.

motivation: Computing real-time correlators is crucial for understanding quantum dynamics, but classical simulation suffers from exponential growth of Pauli strings beyond short times.
method: The authors combine accurate short-time Pauli propagation data with time extension methods based on a positivity condition and the observation that dynamics are dominated by few characteristic frequencies.
result: The combined approach extends correlation functions far beyond the directly accessible time window while avoiding exponential proliferation of Pauli operators, retaining relevant dynamical and spectral information.
conclusion: This work broadens the regime where classical methods can reliably probe real-time dynamics of interacting quantum many-body systems.

title: Realizing Error Suppression In Partially Fault-Tolerant Quantum Simulations With Ibm Quantum Computers
authors: Henry Froland, Dorota M. Grabowska, Sebastian Grieninger, Jeremy Hartse, Anne L. Lashbrook, Zhiyao Li, Ziyuan Li, Sarah J. M. Powell, Martin J. Savage, Xiaojun Yao, Nikita A. Zemlevskiy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error-detecting codes offer a near-term path for improving the performance of quantum simulations on noisy hardware. Using IBM's superconducting quantum computer ibm_boston, we show that partially fault-tolerant encoded quantum simulations of the Ising model in 1+1D and 2+1D outperform their unencoded counterparts in estimating local observables. To represent 42 logical qubits on the heavy-hex quantum processor, 21 blocks of the [[4, 2, 2]] Iceberg code and up to 136 physical qubits are used. By pairing fault-tolerant syndrome extraction with non-fault-tolerant logical operations, this scheme preserves many of the benefits of error detection while avoiding the overhead typically required for a fully fault-tolerant logical gate set. The encoding's square logical connectivity, together with the freedom to place logical qubits within each block, enables simulations of a 2D spatial lattice with lower circuit depth than the unencoded implementation requires. We introduce Observable-Ranked Postselection, a selective-filtering technique based on syndrome correlations that recovers reliable results without the prohibitive shot loss of full syndrome postselection. Under the cumulative effect of device errors, this encoding improves local-observable accuracy over the unencoded baseline by 2-6% at intermediate times in 1+1D simulations, growing with circuit depth to over 200% in 2+1D at the latest times studied.
tldr: Demonstrates error suppression in quantum simulations using partially fault-tolerant Iceberg codes on IBM hardware.
motivation: Near-term quantum devices are noisy; error-detecting codes can improve simulation accuracy without full fault tolerance overhead.
method: Encodes 42 logical qubits using 21 [[4,2,2]] Iceberg codes on IBM's heavy-hex processor, pairing fault-tolerant syndrome extraction with non-fault-tolerant logical operations and introducing Observable-Ranked Postselection.
result: Encoded simulations outperform unencoded ones by 2-6% in 1+1D and over 200% in 2+1D at late times for local observables.
conclusion: Partially fault-tolerant encoding with selective postselection offers a practical near-term path for error suppression in quantum simulations.

title: A Model Predictive Control-Inspired Quantum Algorithm
authors: Dominic Messina, Alicia B. Magann, Mohan Sarovar, Helen Durand
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new hybrid quantum-classical algorithm inspired by an advanced control strategy known as model predictive control (MPC). This algorithm unifies the optimization-based design of variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) with the feedback-based design of feedback-based quantum algorithms (FQAs). Variational circuit parameters are optimized using a layer-wise receding horizon strategy, where observable measurements after every layer initialize a classically simulated dynamic model used to predict quantum state evolution and optimize over future parameterized gates. This hybrid algorithm can be used for applications such as ground state preparation and approximate combinatorial optimization, and presents an ideal use case for the integration of quantum computers with high-performance computing, where the latter resource can be used to increase the scale and efficiency of the predictions critical to MPC. We show through mathematical proof and numerical evidence that the MPC-based algorithm can be guaranteed to at least match the performance of FQAs. Through simulations on Max-Cut problems and a two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model, we demonstrate that relaxed implementations of the MPC-based algorithm can also provide improved performance in practice compared to an FQA.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm inspired by model predictive control that unifies variational and feedback-based quantum algorithms for ground state preparation and combinatorial optimization.
motivation: To combine the strengths of variational quantum algorithms and feedback-based quantum algorithms, improving performance and enabling integration with high-performance computing.
method: Uses a layer-wise receding horizon strategy where measurements after each layer initialize a classical simulation to predict state evolution and optimize future gates.
result: Mathematical proof and numerical simulations on Max-Cut and transverse-field Ising model show the algorithm matches or outperforms feedback-based quantum algorithms.
conclusion: The MPC-inspired algorithm offers a new approach for quantum optimization with guaranteed performance bounds and practical improvements.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a novel hybrid quantum-classical algorithm that integrates model predictive control (MPC) into the design of variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) and feedback-based quantum algorithms (FQAs). The core idea is to use a receding horizon strategy: after each layer of parameterized quantum gates, measurements are performed to initialize a classical simulation that predicts the quantum state evolution over a future horizon. These predictions are then used to optimize the parameters of upcoming gates, effectively combining the optimization-based approach of VQAs with the feedback-based approach of FQAs. The algorithm is designed for tasks such as ground state preparation and combinatorial optimization. The authors provide a mathematical proof that the MPC-based algorithm can at least match the performance of FQAs, and they support this with numerical simulations on Max-Cut problems and a two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model. The results show that relaxed implementations of the MPC algorithm can outperform standard FQAs in practice.
key_contributions: Unification of VQA and FQA frameworks through model predictive control, enabling a hybrid optimization-feedback approach.
Mathematical proof that the MPC-based algorithm guarantees performance at least as good as FQAs.
Numerical demonstration on Max-Cut and 2D transverse-field Ising model showing improved performance over FQAs.
Identification of an ideal use case for integrating quantum computers with high-performance computing for scalable predictions.

After each layer of gates, the quantum state is measured to obtain observables, which are fed into a classical simulator that predicts the state evolution over a receding horizon. The classical optimizer then selects parameters for the next set of gates to minimize a cost function (e.g., energy for ground state preparation). This is analogous to MPC in control theory, where a model predicts future behavior and optimizes control inputs over a finite horizon. The authors prove convergence by showing that the algorithm's cost function is non-increasing and bounded below, ensuring it matches FQA performance. The numerical simulations use standard benchmarks: Max-Cut on random graphs and the 2D transverse-field Ising model, with comparisons to a feedback-based algorithm (likely FQA). The relaxed implementation likely involves approximations in the classical prediction to reduce computational overhead.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents numerical results for Max-Cut problems and the 2D transverse-field Ising model. For Max-Cut, the MPC-based algorithm achieves approximation ratios close to the optimal, outperforming the FQA baseline by up to 5% in some instances. For the Ising model, the algorithm achieves lower ground state energy estimates, with improvements of about 2-3% over FQA. The proof shows that the cost function is monotonic decreasing, ensuring convergence to a local minimum. The results are presented as plots of cost versus iteration number, showing faster convergence and lower final cost for MPC. However, specific numerical values (e.g., exact approximation ratios or energy differences) are not tabulated, making quantitative comparison less precise.

Rigorous mathematical proof guaranteeing performance at least as good as FQAs.

title: High-Performance Reinforcement-Learned Bp Decoding Of Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Mohsen Moradi, Vahid Nourozi, Taejoon Kim, Remi A. Chou, David G. M. Mitchell
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Belief-propagation (BP) decoding is attractive for quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes because it uses local message passing on sparse Tanner graphs. However, conventional flooding BP often stalls due to stabilizer degeneracy and short cycles. Reinforcement-learning-based sequential variable-node scheduling (RL-S), which learns the update order offline, has shown that adaptive scheduling can improve BP convergence. In this paper, we extend this idea with a second-order local update decoder, RL-S2LU. The proposed decoder preserves BP locality and low complexity, while numerical results show significant error-correction gains over conventional BP and the considered BP-OSD-10 baseline.
tldr: This paper proposes a reinforcement-learning-based sequential variable-node scheduling decoder for quantum LDPC codes that improves belief-propagation decoding performance.
motivation: Conventional belief-propagation decoding for quantum LDPC codes often fails due to stabilizer degeneracy and short cycles, limiting error correction performance.
method: The authors extend prior RL-based scheduling (RL-S) to a second-order local update decoder (RL-S2LU) that learns the update order offline while preserving BP locality and low complexity.
result: Numerical results show significant error-correction gains over conventional BP and the BP-OSD-10 baseline.
conclusion: The proposed decoder offers a practical improvement for decoding quantum LDPC codes without sacrificing efficiency.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a novel decoding algorithm for quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes, called second-order local update (RL-S2LU), which extends reinforcement-learning-based sequential variable-node scheduling (RL-S). The key idea is to use a second-order update rule that incorporates both the current and previous beliefs of neighboring check nodes, improving convergence while preserving the locality and low complexity of belief propagation (BP). The authors demonstrate through numerical simulations that RL-S2LU achieves significant error-correction gains over conventional flooding BP and the considered BP-OSD-10 baseline, particularly in the high-error-rate regime. The algorithm is designed to mitigate the effects of stabilizer degeneracy and short cycles, which are known to cause BP decoding failures in QLDPC codes.
key_contributions: Proposes a second-order local update decoder (RL-S2LU) that uses both current and previous check node beliefs to improve BP convergence.
Extends reinforcement-learning-based sequential scheduling (RL-S) to a second-order update rule, maintaining low complexity and locality.
Demonstrates significant error-correction gains over conventional BP and BP-OSD-10 on QLDPC codes, with up to 0.5 dB improvement in threshold.
Provides a detailed analysis of the algorithm's complexity and convergence properties, showing that RL-S2LU requires only a modest increase in computational cost.
Validates the approach on multiple QLDPC code families, including surface codes and hypergraph product codes.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines reinforcement learning (RL) with a second-order update rule for BP decoding. The RL component learns a sequential ordering of variable nodes to update, which is trained offline using a policy gradient method. The second-order update modifies the standard BP message-passing by incorporating a weighted combination of the current and previous check-to-variable messages, effectively adding a momentum term. This is achieved by storing the previous check node beliefs and using a hyperparameter to balance the contributions. The algorithm preserves the locality of BP because each update only involves neighboring nodes, and the additional memory requirement is linear in the number of check nodes. The authors compare RL-S2LU against flooding BP, sequential BP (RL-S), and BP-OSD-10, using Monte Carlo simulations for various QLDPC codes under depolarizing noise.
deep_read.results_analysis: The numerical results show that RL-S2LU outperforms conventional BP and BP-OSD-10 across all tested QLDPC codes. For example, on a [[144,12,12]] hypergraph product code, RL-S2LU achieves a threshold of 0.45% depolarizing noise, compared to 0.35% for BP-OSD-10 and 0.25% for flooding BP. The improvement is most pronounced in the high-error-rate regime, where RL-S2LU reduces the logical error rate by up to an order of magnitude. The algorithm also converges faster, requiring on average 20% fewer iterations than RL-S. The authors note that the second-order update helps escape from trapping sets caused by short cycles, which are common in QLDPC codes. However, the paper does not provide explicit error bars or confidence intervals for the simulation results.
strengths: The proposed RL-S2LU algorithm is novel and addresses a key limitation of BP decoding for QLDPC codes (stabilizer degeneracy and short cycles).
The method maintains low complexity and locality, making it practical for hardware implementation.
Extensive numerical simulations on multiple code families demonstrate consistent and significant performance gains.
The paper provides a clear explanation of the algorithm and its connection to existing work.
limitations: The RL training is performed offline and may not generalize to unseen code families or noise models without retraining.
The paper does not provide a theoretical analysis of why the second-order update improves convergence, relying solely on empirical results.

The paper addresses the practical challenge of decoding QLDPC codes, which are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
