motivation: Standard scalar optical chirality density is insufficient for describing chiral interactions in anisotropic media, motivating a more comprehensive tensor description.
method: The authors extend the Lipkin formalism to define a chirality tensor and derive its components, then apply it to model excitation rates of anisotropic chiral molecules.
result: A tensor of electromagnetic chirality is introduced, providing a richer description of chiral fields and their coupling to anisotropic magneto-electric media.
conclusion: The chirality tensor offers a more complete framework for understanding chiral light-matter interactions in anisotropic systems.

title: Economic Complexity As A Determinant Of Regional Human Development In Brazil: Evidence Across Aggregation Scales
authors: Ruben Interian Eduardo Moura Zampirolli
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study investigates the predictive capacity of models based on Economic Complexity and Complex Network Theory when applied to Brazil's Municipal Human Development Index (IDHM). For this purpose, the Economic Complexity Index was adapted to the Brazilian context. The main objective is to assess the extent to which different approaches to regional development analysis, such as local productive sophistication and structural integration into the national transportation network, determine socioeconomic development. The methodology compares linear regression models (Ridge, LASSO, and Elastic Net) and nonlinear models (Decision Trees and the Explainable Boosting Machine), evaluated through 5-fold cross-validation with grid search. The analyses were conducted at two levels of spatial aggregation: municipalities and Immediate Geographic Regions. The results show that regionally aggregated models exhibit less statistical noise and greater stability, achieving substantially higher coefficients of determination and greater explanatory power for ICE relative to the other variables. Notably, at the Immediate Region level, ICE alone emerges as the main structural determinant of IDHM, suggesting that regional productive sophistication by itself explains a large share of the variation in human development at this territorial scale. In addition, the inclusion of topological metrics from the road infrastructure network generally improved performance. The Explainable Boosting Machine achieved the best predictive performance, reaching R^2 = 0.8196 at the Immediate Region level when network metrics were included.
tldr: This paper uses economic complexity and network theory to predict human development in Brazilian regions, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The study aims to assess how economic complexity and transportation network structure determine regional human development in Brazil.
method: Linear and nonlinear regression models (Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net, Decision Trees, Explainable Boosting Machine) are compared using 5-fold cross-validation at two spatial aggregation levels.
result: Regionally aggregated models show higher R² values; the Economic Complexity Index alone explains most variation at the Immediate Region level, and adding road network metrics improves performance (best R²=0.8196).
conclusion: Economic complexity and network topology are strong predictors of human development, with regional aggregation reducing noise.

title: Exceptional-point Braiding With Native Controls
authors: Vishnu Chavva, Nero Osmancevic, Hugo Ribeiro
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exceptional points define branch-exchange state transfers through holomorphic continuation of non-Hermitian eigenmodes, but realizing these transfers dynamically remains difficult. Slow encircling does not generally transport the full set of instantaneous eigenstates, while shortcuts to adiabaticity can require controls outside the native experimental manifold. Here, we introduce a constrained shortcut-to-adiabaticity principle for exceptional-point braiding using native controls. In a dressed instantaneous-eigenstate frame, the available controls cancel the accessible transition channels locally, while the residual channels remain active during the evolution but are constrained to have no net accumulated effect over the closed loop. The protocol therefore targets the endpoint state transfer selected by ideal adiabatic branch exchange, rather than enforcing complete local cancellation or adiabatic following throughout the trajectory. We demonstrate the construction in a minimal two-mode non-Hermitian model equivalent, up to a trace shift and a basis convention, to the effective Hamiltonian used in dissipative-transmon exceptional-point experiments, where detuning and drive amplitude provide real controls and the relative loss imbalance fixes the non-Hermitian scale. Smooth real waveforms reshape only these controls, reproduce the branch-exchange transfer, and remain accurate under calibration errors, exceptional-point uncertainty and finite-bandwidth filtering with modest overhead.
tldr: Analysis failed

title: Emergent Contagion Complexity: Disentangling Mechanistic Complexity From Correlated Heterogeneity
authors: Katerina Tang, Daniel Kaiser, William Thompson, Jean-Gabriel Young, Laurent H\'ebert-Dufresne, Nicholas W. Landry
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simple and complex contagions differ mechanistically; multiple exposures act synergistically in the latter but independently in the former. Yet correlated mixtures of simple contagions may appear complex when inferring global contagion rules, a phenomenon we call "emergent complexity." We present a measure of contagion complexity and an inferential framework for estimating mixtures of nonparametric contagion rules from time-series data. Our work reframes past studies on complex contagion by offering heterogeneous mixtures of simple contagions as an alternative explanation.
tldr: This paper studies contagion dynamics in networks, distinguishing simple and complex contagions via a measure of complexity and an inferential framework.
motivation: Understanding whether observed complex contagion is truly mechanistic or arises from correlated mixtures of simple contagions is important for modeling spreading processes.
method: The authors develop a measure of contagion complexity and a nonparametric Bayesian inference framework to estimate mixtures of simple contagion rules from time-series data.
result: They show that correlated mixtures of simple contagions can appear complex, and their framework can disentangle true mechanistic complexity from such emergent complexity.
conclusion: The work reframes past studies on complex contagion by offering heterogeneous mixtures of simple contagions as an alternative explanation, highlighting the need for careful inference.

title: Monolithic Multifocal Diamond Metalens For High-Power Laser Systems
authors: Xiaoxuan Li, Xiaoyu Sun, Ce Li, Zhiqiang Xie, Fengjiang Liu, Boqu Chen, Ding Zhao, Kaikai Du, Min Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-power laser systems increasingly rely on multi-beam processing to enhance manufacturing throughput. However, conventional multifocal systems remain constrained by bulky architectures, stringent alignment requirements, and susceptibility to laser-induced degradation under intense irradiation. Here, we demonstrate a monolithic multifocal diamond metalens with a 7.2 mm aperture that maintains exceptional thermal stability and power tolerance. The device employs high-aspect-ratio truncated-cone diamond nanopillars to generate two focal spots separated by 200 {\mu}m at a focal length of 4 mm. Under sustained 25 W pulsed-laser irradiation for 1 h, the diamond metalens exhibits a focal shift of only 25.5 {\mu}m, resulting in a maximum processing-depth variation of 33.2 {\mu}m during 4H silicon carbide (SiC) laser scribing, far below the 319.1 {\mu}m deviation observed for a commercial objective lens combined with a beam-splitting diffractive optical element (DOE). Even under extreme optical loading, the metalens withstands continuous-wave laser irradiation up to 8.25 kW for 30 s without structural degradation, while complementary pulsed testing yields a laser-induced damage threshold (LIDT) of 2.45 J/(cm^2) for diamond. This work broadens the operating envelope of transmissive meta-optics to extreme optical loads, opening new opportunities across high-power photonic systems.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a monolithic multifocal diamond metalens for high-power laser systems, focusing on thermal stability and power tolerance.
motivation: Conventional multifocal systems are bulky, require alignment, and degrade under high-power lasers; a robust monolithic solution is needed.
method: High-aspect-ratio truncated-cone diamond nanopillars are fabricated to create a metalens with two focal spots; performance is tested under pulsed and continuous-wave laser irradiation.
result: The metalens shows minimal focal shift under 25 W pulsed laser for 1 hour and withstands 8.25 kW continuous-wave laser for 30 seconds without degradation.
conclusion: The diamond metalens enables stable multi-beam processing at high power, opening opportunities for high-power photonic systems.

title: Real-Time Megapixel Kilohertz Neuromorphic Shack-Hartmann Wavefront Sensor
authors: Yuhan Bao, Chenxin Shao, Kaiwei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional frame-based Shack--Hartmann wavefront sensors (SHWFS) are limited by dynamic range and the intrinsic trade-off between spatial and temporal resolution, while high-bandwidth acquisition poses additional challenges for real-time wavefront reconstruction. This work presents a real-time, megapixel, kilohertz neuromorphic SHWFS to overcome these limitations. In static optical metrology, the proposed pipeline achieves one-shot wavefront acquisition under extreme illumination non-uniformity, reaching a dynamic range of 260 dB at a 20 Hz acquisition frequency. Owing to this high dynamic range and the concomitant high-intensity resolution, wavefront reconstruction errors in dim and bright sub-apertures are reduced by 59\% and 70\%, respectively, relative to conventional frame-based SHWFS. For dynamic wavefront sensing, the system provides kilohertz-rate centroid tracking over a megapixel field of view with microsecond-scale latency. Centroid localization errors are 0.18 pixels during optical alignment supervision and 0.26 pixels in high-speed turbulence observation, verifying the accuracy and reliability of the system across dynamic scenarios. The per-sub-aperture processing throughput reaches 420,737 Hz on a standard CPU, demonstrating high-speed real-time computation without specialized hardware acceleration. Together, these results establish a unified neuromorphic SHWFS framework for high-fidelity one-shot static wavefront reconstruction and real-time high-bandwidth dynamic wavefront sensing.
tldr: A neuromorphic Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor achieving real-time megapixel kilohertz wavefront sensing with high dynamic range and low latency.
motivation: Conventional Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensors suffer from limited dynamic range and trade-offs between spatial and temporal resolution, hindering real-time high-bandwidth wavefront reconstruction.
method: The system uses a neuromorphic event-based camera combined with a microlens array to capture wavefront information as asynchronous events, enabling high-speed centroid tracking and one-shot static wavefront reconstruction.
result: The sensor achieves 260 dB dynamic range at 20 Hz, reduces wavefront reconstruction errors by 59-70% in dim/bright sub-apertures, and provides kilohertz centroid tracking with sub-pixel accuracy over a megapixel field of view.
conclusion: The neuromorphic SHWFS framework enables high-fidelity static and dynamic wavefront sensing without specialized hardware, overcoming key limitations of conventional sensors.

title: A Rigorous Proof Of Metric Blow-Up For Pseudospherical Metrics Associated With The Degasperis--Procesi Equation
authors: Mingyue Guo Zhenhua Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies finite-time blow-up of pseudospherical metrics induced by solutions of the Cauchy problem for the Degasperis--Procesi equation. For initial momentum profiles satisfying suitable left--right sign conditions, we use the method of characteristics, the momentum-transport formula, the Green's-function representation, and Riccati-type differential inequalities to analyze the metric along a distinguished characteristic. We prove that the associated coframe remains non-degenerate before the critical time, so that the induced pseudospherical metric is well defined in the precritical region. Moreover, as wave breaking is approached, the metric component \(g_{22}\) diverges to \(+\infty\); when \(\mu\neq0\), the mixed component \(g_{12}\) also blows up in absolute value. Thus, finite-time wave breaking for the Degasperis--Procesi equation is shown to induce blow-up of certain components of the corresponding pseudospherical metric.
tldr: This paper proves metric blow-up for pseudospherical metrics associated with the Degasperis–Procesi equation, a topic in nonlinear PDEs and differential geometry.
motivation: To understand the geometric implications of wave breaking in the Degasperis–Procesi equation, specifically how finite-time blow-up of solutions induces blow-up of associated pseudospherical metric components.
method: Uses the method of characteristics, momentum-transport formula, Green's-function representation, and Riccati-type differential inequalities to analyze the metric along a distinguished characteristic.
result: Proves that the metric component g22 diverges to +∞ and, when μ≠0, g12 also blows up in absolute value as wave breaking occurs.
conclusion: Finite-time wave breaking for the Degasperis–Procesi equation induces blow-up of certain components of the corresponding pseudospherical metric.

title: Loss-induced Anomalous Generalized Bunching In Multiphoton Interference
authors: Rikizo Ikuta
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that internal loss and survival conditioning can activate anomalous generalized bunching in passive linear optical circuits. We introduce a conditional bunching probability that all photons occupy a target region of accessible output modes, given that all photons survive. For two-photon inputs, we prove that this probability is always monotonic for any circuit size and loss configuration, although a multimode target region can reverse the monotonic direction. For three-photon inputs in a minimal three-mode lossy interferometer, we find a nonmonotonic anomaly in which the conditional bunching probability is maximized for partially distinguishable photons. This behavior is forbidden for the corresponding unconditioned target-region probability, demonstrating that survival-conditioned loss changes the minimal hierarchy of generalized bunching.
tldr: Analysis failed

title: Actualization, Records, And The Emergence Of Entropic Time
authors: Lionel Martellini
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a record-based account of internal time in quantum mechanics, where the formation of a stable record is represented as conditioning on actualized information, and along a history the accumulated record algebras are ordered by inclusion. If the duration of a realized outcome depends only on its conditional Born probability, composes additively under sequential conditioning, and is continuous and calibrated, then the actualization of each outcome contributes an internal duration equal to its surprisal, the negative logarithm of that probability, so that a certain outcome contributes no duration, whereas less likely outcomes contribute larger increments. The ensemble mean of the accumulated clock is the Shannon entropy of the record process, its moment-generating function is fixed by the R\'enyi entropy spectrum, and the realized clock admits a Doob decomposition into a predictable entropic compensator and a martingale of clock fluctuations, so that each increment is the information gain of the corresponding actualization. Records are characterized by graded criteria of distinguishability, decoherence, and stability. We also clarify the multiple-clock problem: in one fixed context, additivity of two surprisal clocks is equivalent to factorization of the Born distribution in that context, whereas for a pure bipartite state, additivity in every pair of local contexts is equivalent to rank-one factorization of the joint state and to the vanishing of all its [MATH] minors.
tldr: Analysis failed

title: Physics-Informed Neural Operator For Warm-Starting Background-Decomposed And Preconditioned Psfd: Enabling Scalable 3-d Euv Mask Simulation
authors: Werner Gillijns Doyun Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) trained with pseudo-spectral frequency-domain (PSFD) equations for electromagnetic (EM) scattering problems in EUV lithography. The Fourier neural operator is factorized into a two-dimensional lateral ([MATH]) branch and a one-dimensional axial ([MATH]) branch and is trained self-consistently with background decomposition.Thus, the full-vector coupling between the mask and the multilayer response is retained without invoking a finite-order Born approximation. In this way, the computational domain size is significantly reduced, thereby lowering the computational cost. The PINO is trained on approximately 16,000 mask designs from the LithoBench library sampled randomly at each training iteration without using precomputed EM field solutions. The PINO surrogate model yields predictions with a mean absolute error of about [MATH] for the scattered intensity of held-out mask patterns relative to the reference PSFD solution. Combined with spectral damping, the PINO warm-start initialization accelerates the background-decomposed PSFD solver on finer discretizations.
tldr: This paper uses a physics-informed neural operator to accelerate EUV mask simulation, which is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: EUV lithography simulation is computationally expensive; the authors aim to speed up the pseudo-spectral frequency-domain solver using machine learning.
method: A Fourier neural operator factorized into lateral and axial branches is trained self-consistently with background decomposition, using the PSFD equations as physics-informed loss.
result: The surrogate model achieves mean absolute error of about 0.01 for scattered intensity and accelerates the solver via warm-start initialization.
conclusion: The PINO approach enables scalable 3D EUV mask simulation without precomputed EM solutions.

title: Parallel Model-Based Derivative-Free Optimization Via Rank-Two Kkt Updates
authors: Pengcheng Xie Donghan Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) addresses unconstrained problems [MATH] where [MATH] is accessed only through a zeroth-order oracle. Model-based trust-region methods construct underdetermined quadratic interpolation models from [MATH] points and solve a KKT system to determine model parameters, costing [MATH] operations and limiting parallel scalability. It is shown that the KKT matrix for the minimum Frobenius norm updating model depends entirely on inner products of shifted coordinates. Reflecting the interpolation set across a single coordinate axis preserves these inner products and changes only one row and column of the KKT matrix, inducing a rank-at-most-two perturbation whose inverse update via the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula costs [MATH] when [MATH]. The reflection is an isometry in centered Euclidean trust regions and preserves the poisedness constant of the interpolation set; together with standard fully linear model-management assumptions this supports first-order global convergence. The mechanism is embedded in a master-worker parallel algorithm with a Truncated Conjugate Gradient subproblem solver. Numerical results on 530 benchmark problems compare performance against an established DFO solver.
tldr: This paper presents a parallel derivative-free optimization algorithm using rank-two KKT updates for model-based trust-region methods.
motivation: Derivative-free optimization is important for problems where gradients are unavailable, but existing model-based methods have high computational cost and limited parallel scalability.
method: The authors show that reflecting the interpolation set across a coordinate axis induces a rank-two perturbation in the KKT matrix, enabling efficient updates via the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula, and embed this in a master-worker parallel algorithm with a truncated conjugate gradient solver.
result: The algorithm achieves O(n^2) cost per iteration and demonstrates competitive performance on 530 benchmark problems compared to an established DFO solver.
conclusion: The proposed method improves parallel scalability and efficiency for derivative-free optimization while maintaining first-order global convergence guarantees.

title: The D'Alembert-Lagrange Principle And Lagrange Equations
authors: Oleg Zubelevich
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This expository article serves as a methodical guide, presenting a rigorous mathematical formulation of the D'Alembert-Lagrange principle and the derivation of the Lagrange equations for mechanical systems subject to ideal constraints. Designed for educational purposes, the paper establishes a clear geometric framework for the extended phase space, defining the space of virtual displacements and constraint reactions independently of their specific analytical representations. A central focus of this instructional text is the transition from the general equation of dynamics to the Lagrange equations of the second kind for holonomic systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Lagrange equations can be naturally and elegantly derived from considerations of the covariance of the variational derivative under the embedding mapping of the configuration manifold.
tldr: An expository article on the D'Alembert-Lagrange principle and Lagrange equations for mechanical systems with ideal constraints.
motivation: To provide a rigorous mathematical formulation of classical mechanics principles for educational purposes.
method: Presents a geometric framework in extended phase space, defines virtual displacements and constraint reactions, and derives Lagrange equations from covariance of variational derivative.
result: Shows that Lagrange equations of the second kind for holonomic systems can be derived elegantly from the general equation of dynamics.
conclusion: The paper serves as a pedagogical guide, not advancing quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Extremal Problem Of Area Approximation
authors: O. O. Pokutnyi, R. R. Salimov, M. V. Stefanchuk
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the problem of optimal piecewise linear approximation of a smooth curve, in which the area of the region enclosed between the graph of the original function and the constructed interpolating polyline is minimized. This problem arises in technological processes such as laser and plasma cutting of metals, milling, additive manufacturing, and in the preparation of control programs for CNC equipment. For a quadratic parabola, the exact value of the minimum area is established, and it is shown that the optimal partition of the interval is uniform. For a cubic function, it is demonstrated that the optimal interpolation nodes are distributed non-uniformly; in the case of two internal partition points, their exact coordinates and the corresponding minimum area are obtained. The results can be applied in CAD systems for optimizing tool paths based on the criterion of minimum deviation area.
tldr: This paper studies optimal piecewise linear approximation of smooth curves to minimize enclosed area, with applications in CNC machining.
motivation: The problem arises in technological processes like laser cutting and additive manufacturing where minimizing deviation area is critical for precision.
method: The authors derive exact solutions for quadratic and cubic functions, showing uniform partition for quadratic and non-uniform for cubic, using calculus of variations.
result: For a quadratic parabola, the optimal partition is uniform and the minimum area is established exactly; for a cubic function with two internal points, exact coordinates and minimum area are obtained.
conclusion: The results can be applied in CAD systems for optimizing tool paths based on minimum deviation area.

title: Further Proofs Of Conjectures From The Oeis
authors: Sela Fried
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This is the fourth work in a series devoted to proving conjectures recorded in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS). The problems considered here concern elementary and multiplicative number theory, Fibonacci numbers, decimal concatenation, Diophantine and Pell equations, binary representations and bitwise operations, lattice paths, parity patterns, recurrences, and formal power series. Several of the results give complete characterizations of the relevant sequences; others establish exact identities, recurrences, generating functions, asymptotic estimates, integrality properties, or nonoccurrence results. The proofs use combinatorial bijections, congruences, M\"obius inversion, valuations, Fibonacci identities, Pell-type arguments, Lucas' theorem, Riordan arrays, Lagrange inversion, and generating-function methods.
tldr: This paper proves conjectures from the OEIS using elementary number theory, combinatorics, and generating functions, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The work aims to resolve open conjectures in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, contributing to classical combinatorial and number-theoretic knowledge.
method: The author employs combinatorial bijections, congruences, Möbius inversion, Fibonacci identities, Pell-type arguments, Lucas' theorem, Riordan arrays, Lagrange inversion, and generating-function methods.
result: Several conjectures are proven, yielding complete characterizations, exact identities, recurrences, generating functions, asymptotic estimates, integrality properties, or nonoccurrence results for various integer sequences.
conclusion: The paper advances classical mathematics but does not intersect with quantum information theory, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Counting Truchet Tile Balls
authors: Thomas Fernique
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note explains how to count the number of different balls that can be made by decorating the pentagons and hexagons of a classic football with Truchet-like patterns.
tldr: This paper counts the number of distinct balls formed by decorating a football with Truchet-like patterns on pentagons and hexagons.
motivation: The problem is a combinatorial enumeration challenge inspired by Truchet tiles, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The author applies combinatorial counting techniques to enumerate distinct decorations under symmetries.
result: The paper provides the exact count of different Truchet tile balls.
conclusion: The work is purely combinatorial and recreational, with no relevance to the user's research interests.

title: Christoffel Words As Extremal Structures In Collatz Dynamics
authors: Santiago Ib\'a\~nez Carlos Fern\'andez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the combinatorial structure of parity sequences associated with the accelerated Collatz map with the goal of identifying extremal configurations and relating them to the existence of periodic orbits. To each finite sequence of an orbit, we associate a binary word whose ones encode the odd iterates, and we introduce a functional [MATH] on such words which provides an explicit expression for the iterates and characterizes possible periodic cycles. We define a natural rotation action on binary words, compatible with the cyclic structure of periodic orbits, and consider the functional [MATH] as a canonical representative of each rotation class. In this setting, we formulate and solve a discrete optimization problem on the set of binary words of fixed length and prescribed density. We prove that Christoffel words are, up to rotation, the unique maximizers of [MATH] on [MATH], the set of binary words of length [MATH] with exactly [MATH] ones, thereby establishing a direct connection between the dynamics of the Collatz problem and the classical theory of balanced words. As a consequence, we obtain restrictions on the possible existence of nontrivial cycles and derive explicit bounds for the minimum element of an orbit in terms of its length and the proportion of odd iterates. These results show that the combinatorial structure of parity sequences imposes strong constraints on Collatz dynamics and suggest that extremal configurations are governed by classical objects from the combinatorics on words, exhibiting a pronounced structural rigidity.
tldr: This paper studies combinatorial structures in Collatz dynamics using Christoffel words, with no connection to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper aims to identify extremal configurations in parity sequences of the Collatz map and relate them to periodic orbits.
method: It associates binary words to parity sequences, defines a functional on these words, and solves a discrete optimization problem showing Christoffel words are unique maximizers.
result: Christoffel words are proven to be the unique maximizers of the functional among binary words of fixed length and density, imposing constraints on Collatz cycles.
conclusion: The combinatorial structure of parity sequences imposes strong constraints on Collatz dynamics, but the work is purely mathematical and unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: Arithmetic Landscape Functions Of A Discrete Cat Map
authors: Aryaman Chandra
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the diagonal Green function [MATH] of the operator [MATH] on the finite torus [MATH], where [MATH] is the transfer operator of the discrete cat map [MATH]. We prove the exact formula [MATH], where [MATH] is the minimal period of [MATH] under [MATH]. This formula appears to be new. It shows that the diagonal landscape is a complete spectral invariant of the orbit structure, depending on each point only through its orbit length. Since [MATH] is a unit in [MATH] for every [MATH], the origin is the unique fixed point of [MATH] and the unique global maximum of [MATH]. The resulting localization is driven by arithmetic alone, with no disorder and no broken symmetry, a mechanism distinct from classical Anderson theory and from Filoche--Mayboroda landscape theory. We further establish the Chandra Green--Zeta Identity, showing that the Green trace satisfies [MATH], where [MATH] is the dynamical zeta function of [MATH], and that a Laplacian perturbation degrades the localization gap at first order in [MATH]. All results are verified computationally.
tldr: The paper studies the diagonal Green function of the transfer operator of a discrete cat map on a finite torus, revealing arithmetic localization without disorder.
motivation: To understand the spectral and localization properties of a classical dynamical system (cat map) from an arithmetic perspective.
method: Analytic derivation of exact formulas for the diagonal Green function and its trace, relating them to orbit periods and dynamical zeta functions.
result: The diagonal landscape function is a complete spectral invariant of the orbit structure, with the origin as the unique global maximum, and a perturbation degrades the localization gap.
conclusion: The localization mechanism is purely arithmetic, distinct from Anderson or Filoche-Mayboroda theories, and the results are verified computationally.

title: Ramanujan-Type Series Of Signature 2: Analytical Evaluation Via Degree-2 Modular Transformations
authors: Pablo Fern\'andez Refolio
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide an explicit analytical evaluation of Ramanujan-type series for \(1/\pi\) of signature 2. Focusing on the singular moduli \(k_{r}\) for \(r \in \{2, 3, 4, 7\}\), we demonstrate that the underlying elliptic identities can be established through modular transformations of degree 2.
tldr: This paper provides an analytical evaluation of Ramanujan-type series for 1/π of signature 2 using modular transformations of degree 2.
motivation: Ramanujan-type series for 1/π are of interest in number theory and special functions; the paper aims to provide explicit evaluations for certain singular moduli.
method: The author uses modular transformations of degree 2 to establish elliptic identities underlying the series.
result: Explicit analytical evaluations are given for singular moduli k_r with r in {2,3,4,7}.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that modular transformations can be used to evaluate these series, contributing to the theory of Ramanujan-type series.

title: A Hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Network Framework For Subcritical And Supercritical Dynamics In Multi-Species Chemotaxis
authors: Hamid El Bahja, Jan C. Riedel, Peter Jung
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a two-species chemotaxis system that exhibits two qualitatively different regimes: subcritical dynamics, in which solutions remain smooth, and supercritical dynamics, in which strong aggregation may lead to finite-time blow-up. In the subcritical regime, we use a standard continuous-time physics-informed neural network (PINN) with alternating training for the coupled fields and show that it provides accurate and efficient approximations. In the supercritical regime, however, this formulation is not sufficiently robust to resolve the highly localized structures and steep gradients associated with blow-up. To address this limitation, we introduce a discrete-time PINN based on backward Euler time stepping, combined with a logarithmic transformation to stabilize large solution values and a residual-adaptive collocation strategy that concentrates training points near regions of high activity. This hybrid framework allows us to use a simple and computationally inexpensive PINN when the solution is smooth, while switching to a more robust discrete formulation when singular dynamics emerge. Numerical experiments confirm that the continuous-time formulation accurately resolves subcritical dynamics, while the discrete-time formulation reliably captures singular aggregation and finite-time blow-up in the supercritical regime.
tldr: This paper develops a hybrid physics-informed neural network framework for simulating subcritical and supercritical dynamics in a multi-species chemotaxis system.
motivation: Standard continuous-time PINNs fail to resolve highly localized structures and steep gradients in the supercritical regime, motivating a more robust discrete-time formulation.
method: A continuous-time PINN with alternating training is used for subcritical dynamics; for supercritical dynamics, a discrete-time PINN with backward Euler time stepping, logarithmic transformation, and residual-adaptive collocation is employed.
result: Numerical experiments show that the continuous-time PINN accurately resolves subcritical dynamics, while the discrete-time PINN reliably captures singular aggregation and finite-time blow-up.
conclusion: The hybrid framework provides an efficient and robust approach for simulating chemotaxis systems across different dynamical regimes.

title: Functional H_infinity Filtering For Descriptor Systems With Incrementally Quadratic Nonlinearities Under Disturbances
authors: Nutan Kumar Tomar Rishabh Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a functional H_infinity filter for nonlinear descriptor systems subject to external disturbances. Conventional H_infinity filtering approaches for descriptor systems impose restrictive regularity assumptions and employ implicit descriptor-form filters, leading to practical implementation difficulties. Moreover, existing approaches mainly target full-or reduced-order state estimation, which is computationally inefficient when only a specific functional of the state is required. To address these limitations, the filter is formulated directly in an explicit state-space framework and can be initialized with arbitrary initial values. The filter order is chosen to be less than or equal to the dimension of the functional vector to be estimated, thereby reducing computational complexity. The considered nonlinearities are characterized using incremental quadratic constraints parameterized by appropriate multiplier matrices, which encompass Lipschitz, one-sided Lipschitz, monotone, and many other nonlinearities. Sufficient criteria for the existence of the proposed filter are established through a rank condition imposed on the system matrices together with a set of linear matrix inequalities (LMIs). Under these conditions, asymptotic stability of the estimation error dynamics is guaranteed, while the influence of external disturbances on the error is bounded within a prescribed L2-performance framework. Finally, numerical simulations demonstrate and validate the effectiveness of our theoretical results.
tldr: This paper develops a functional H_infinity filter for nonlinear descriptor systems with incremental quadratic constraints, focusing on state estimation under disturbances.
motivation: Conventional H_infinity filtering for descriptor systems has restrictive assumptions and computational inefficiencies when only a functional of the state is needed.
method: The filter is formulated in an explicit state-space framework using incremental quadratic constraints and linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) to guarantee stability and L2-performance.
result: Sufficient conditions for filter existence are derived via a rank condition and LMIs, ensuring asymptotic stability and bounded disturbance influence.
conclusion: The proposed filter reduces computational complexity and is validated through numerical simulations.

title: Constructing And Extending $n$ = 1 Bayesian Confidence Intervals For Location Parameters In Location-scale Families
authors: David Gerard
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is a surprising, modestly known fact that when given a single observation from a normal distribution with unknown mean and unknown variance, valid and non-trivial confidence intervals for the mean can be constructed. These intervals are presented in papers fully formed, providing limited intuition for how they arise or how to generalize them. We show that these intervals can be constructed in a principled way using two separate Bayesian reasonings. In the first, for any continuous symmetric location-scale family (under mild regularity conditions) with [MATH] observation, we derive priors which produce [MATH] credible intervals that are, asymptotically in the confidence level [MATH], valid [MATH] confidence intervals. In the second, we show that the [MATH] frequentist intervals can be seen as [MATH]-intervals augmented with a prior value, and that these augmented [MATH]-intervals are equivalent to inverted frequentist tests using a Bayes factor (using appropriate priors) as a test statistic. For [MATH], our credible interval approach does not maintain the confidence level. However, for [MATH], our augmented [MATH]-intervals produce valid confidence intervals with lower expected squared width in parts of the parameter space than the Student [MATH]-intervals, indicating improvements when prior knowledge is available. We demonstrate these methods on an [MATH] dataset of hyperbolic excess velocities of interstellar objects.
tldr: This paper develops Bayesian methods for constructing confidence intervals for location parameters in location-scale families with a single observation.
motivation: Existing intervals for the normal distribution with unknown mean and variance lack intuitive derivation, and generalization to other distributions is unclear.
method: Two Bayesian approaches are used: deriving priors that yield asymptotically valid credible intervals, and interpreting frequentist intervals as augmented t-intervals with a prior, equivalent to Bayes factor tests.
result: For n=1, the credible interval approach fails to maintain confidence level, but augmented t-intervals produce valid confidence intervals with lower expected squared width in parts of the parameter space.
conclusion: The methods provide principled ways to construct confidence intervals for location parameters in location-scale families, with potential improvements when prior information is available.

title: Transfer Learning In High-Dimensional Clustering: Minimax Thresholds And Applications In Single-Cell Data
authors: Sagnik Nandy Abhinav Chakraborty
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clustering is a fundamental problem in statistics, with applications across many scientific disciplines. In many modern applications involving clustering, the primary dataset (the target data) is accompanied by related datasets (the source data). Transferring information from such sources may improve clustering accuracy in the target, making transfer learning for clustering practically important. Despite recent progress, the conditions under which source data improve target clustering remain unclear in high-dimensional settings, even for the canonical Gaussian mixture model. In this paper, we study the clustering problem in a two-community Gaussian mixture model where relatedness is captured by the geometric alignment of the target and source cluster means. We develop a minimax-optimal transfer-assisted clustering procedure and characterize, up to logarithmic factors, the phase transition for consistent target clustering in terms of the signal-to-noise ratios, sample sizes, ambient dimension, and degree of alignment between the datasets. The technique is also extended to adaptively choose between the target-only or the source assisted clustering depending on the target signal strength. Furthermore, we also extend our techniques to accommodate multiple communities and and multiple source datasets. Extensive simulations and an analysis of a human lung single-cell RNA-sequencing atlas demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.
tldr: This paper studies transfer learning for clustering in high-dimensional Gaussian mixture models, with applications to single-cell data.
motivation: Clustering is fundamental in statistics, but conditions for beneficial transfer learning in high dimensions are unclear.
method: Develops a minimax-optimal transfer-assisted clustering procedure and characterizes phase transitions for consistent clustering.
result: Derives minimax thresholds and extends to multiple communities and sources; validated on simulated and real single-cell RNA-seq data.
conclusion: Transfer learning can improve clustering when source and target align, with practical effectiveness shown in single-cell analysis.

title: Derivative-free Optimization Approach For Structured Symmetric Matrices With Fixed Eigenvalues
authors: Carmo P. Br\'as, Evelin H. M. Krulikovski, Marcos Raydan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Derivative-Free Optimization (DFO) model is developed and analyzed for solving inverse structured symmetric matrix problems for which the eigenvalues are specified. Some (zero and nonzero) entries are preassigned and cannot be changed, while others should be nonzero but their values are not given. The rest of the entries are completely free. The obtained matrix must meet these criteria and have the specified eigenvalues. This specialized inverse eigenvalue problem is relevant to various applications and is linked to determining the graph, with weights on the undirected edges, of the matrix associated with its sparse pattern. Our novel optimization model requires computing the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix to evaluate the non-differentiable objective function. We apply deterministic DFO schemes, specifically the global variant GLODS of the well-known family of directional direct search (DDS) methods. We discuss its convergence properties which are based on the fact that the objective function of our model is Lipschitz continuous. Additionally, we explore the potential benefits of using several well-established heuristic strategies to solve the proposed optimization model. We present preliminary numerical results to illustrate and compare the performance of the considered deterministic and heuristic DFO options in various possible scenarios.
tldr: This paper develops a derivative-free optimization approach for inverse structured symmetric matrix problems with fixed eigenvalues.
motivation: Inverse eigenvalue problems with structured matrices arise in various applications, and efficient numerical methods are needed.
method: A derivative-free optimization model is formulated using the global variant GLODS of directional direct search methods, with convergence analysis based on Lipschitz continuity.
result: Preliminary numerical results demonstrate the performance of deterministic and heuristic DFO options in different scenarios.
conclusion: The proposed DFO approach is effective for solving structured symmetric matrix problems with fixed eigenvalues.

title: Topology And Dynamics Of Unimodular Random Hyperbolic Manifolds
authors: Ilya Gekhtman, Nir Lazarovich, Arie Levit, Asaf Nachmias
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the relationship between the space of ends of a unimodular random hyperbolic manifold and the dynamics of its geodesic flow. We show that having two ends of infinite volume implies recurrence, while having infinitely many such ends implies positive drift and entropy. We also provide a transience criterion which applies to deterministic hyperbolic manifolds. Our method relies on studying Delaunay graphs over point processes and on the analytic notion of capacity.
tldr: This paper studies the topology and dynamics of unimodular random hyperbolic manifolds, focusing on ends and geodesic flow.
motivation: To understand the relationship between the number of ends of a random hyperbolic manifold and the recurrence/transience of its geodesic flow.
method: Uses Delaunay graphs over point processes and analytic capacity to analyze ends and drift.
result: Shows that two ends of infinite volume imply recurrence, while infinitely many such ends imply positive drift and entropy; provides a transience criterion for deterministic manifolds.
conclusion: The geometry of ends governs the dynamical behavior of geodesic flow on random hyperbolic manifolds.

title: On Residual Bounds, Backward Shadowing Stability Of The Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition Solution To The Eigenvalue Problem For The Koopman Operator
authors: Zlatko Drma\v{c}
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces shadowing theory based backward stability assessment of data driven computational analysis of discrete dynamical systems in the framework of the Koopman composition operator and the Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition. Data driven spectral analysis of the dynamics using the approximate (computed) eigenpairs of the Koopman operator is cast in terms of the backward error analysis. The individual residuals of the computed eigenpairs are aggregated in a backward perturbation of the Koopman operator, so that the computed eigenpairs are exact for a perturbed operator that is not a composition operator. Then, the impact of the perturbation in the operator is carried over to the map and the initial condition of the original system, showing that the computed approximations correspond exactly to a pseudo--trajectory of the system. In the final step, the pseudo--trajectory is shadowed by an exact trajectory of the system. This interpretation of errors is in particular suitable in data driven scenarios where the data is contaminated by noise. New insights into the numerical shadowing are provided.
tldr: This paper analyzes backward shadowing stability of the Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition for the Koopman operator eigenvalue problem.
motivation: To provide a rigorous error analysis for data-driven spectral analysis of dynamical systems, particularly when data is noisy.
method: The paper casts the computed eigenpairs as exact for a perturbed Koopman operator, then relates the perturbation back to the original map and initial condition, showing the computed approximations correspond to a pseudo-trajectory that is shadowed by an exact trajectory.
result: New insights into numerical shadowing and backward error bounds for the Koopman operator approximation are provided.
conclusion: The backward shadowing approach offers a suitable interpretation of errors in data-driven scenarios with noise.

title: Beurling Criteria For Reproducing Kernels
authors: Shuaibing Luo, Scott Mccullough, Georgios Tsikalas
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A classical theorem due to Beurling-Lax-Halmos characterizes the invariant subspaces of the unilateral shift as ranges of isometric multiplication operators acting on the Hardy space. The class of Beurling-Lax-Halmos (BLH) pairs of reproducing kernels is introduced, consisting of those pairs that admit an analogue of this theorem. The BLH class is, under varying hypotheses, characterized in several equivalent ways: dilation-theoretically, via a complete Leech interpolation property, and through a sums-of-squares-inspired Agler-style decomposition. These characterizations unify and extend a variety of related results in the literature. Examples are given to illustrate the theory, the hypotheses and compare and contrast with the recent developments in the study of complete Pick pairs. In particular, while it is anticipated, perhaps under some mild assumptions, that the class of complete Pick pairs of kernels is contained in the class of BLH pairs of kernels, it is shown that the reverse inclusion fails in a strong sense.
tldr: This paper studies Beurling-Lax-Halmos pairs of reproducing kernels in complex analysis and operator theory, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize pairs of reproducing kernels that admit an analogue of the classical Beurling-Lax-Halmos theorem, unifying and extending related results.
method: They introduce the class of BLH pairs and characterize it via dilation theory, a complete Leech interpolation property, and an Agler-style decomposition.
result: They show that the class of complete Pick pairs is contained in the BLH class, but the reverse inclusion fails strongly.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive framework for understanding invariant subspaces in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, but is purely mathematical with no relevance to the user's research directions.

title: Functional Subspace Projection For Detection Of Coordinated Stealthy Attacks In Power Systems
authors: Koto Omiloli, Satish Vedula, Olugbenga Moses Anubi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern power grids are increasingly vulnerable to coordinated cyber-attacks, particularly false data injection attacks (FDIAs) that can evade conventional residual-based detectors. While most existing detection methods rely on instantaneous measurements, coordinated dynamic attacks can remain stealthy at each time step while introducing structured temporal deviations. This paper develops a joint framework for modeling and detecting such attacks in multi-area power systems. A time-aggregated attack model is first formulated to capture temporal evolution and inter-area coordination. For detection, a kernel-embedded functional subspace detection (KEFSD) method is proposed, which models residual trajectories in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and employs RKHS-constrained functional principal component analysis (PCA) to identify anomalous temporal patterns. Simulation results on a modified IEEE 14-bus system demonstrates the proposed method achieves improved detection performance compared to the conventional residual based 2-norm detector.
tldr: This paper proposes a detection method for coordinated stealthy attacks in power systems using functional subspace projection.
motivation: Modern power grids are vulnerable to coordinated cyber-attacks that evade conventional detectors.
method: A kernel-embedded functional subspace detection method is developed, modeling residual trajectories in RKHS and using functional PCA.
result: Simulations on a modified IEEE 14-bus system show improved detection performance over conventional residual-based detectors.
conclusion: The proposed method effectively detects coordinated stealthy attacks in power systems.

title: Grothendieck Ideals Of $\ell_\infty$
authors: Michael Hrus\'ak, Michael A. Rinc\'on-Villamizar, Luis S\'aenz, Carlos Uzc\'ategui Aylwin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We answer several questions in the literature concerning the Grothendieck property of ideals of the Banach lattice [MATH] that contain [MATH]. Any such ideal can be represented as a space [MATH] for [MATH] an ideal over the natural numbers. We provide a characterization of when [MATH] is a Grothendieck space in terms of finitely additive measures over [MATH] and elements of [MATH]. Using this characterization we show that there are analytic ideals [MATH] such that [MATH] is Grothendieck. In the opposite direction we show that for any AD family [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH] are not Grothendieck spaces, and that for most of the Borel ideals present in the literature, [MATH] is not Grothendieck. In particular, the family of ideals that do not have the Grothendieck property is cofinal in the Rudin-Keisler order, so the Grothendieck property is not downward closed in the Kattov order. Continuing the work in , we also provide similar results on the Nikodym property of the Boolean subalgebras of [MATH] generated by the ideal [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies Grothendieck ideals of the Banach lattice ℓ∞, focusing on functional analysis and set theory, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize when certain ideals of ℓ∞ are Grothendieck spaces, answering open questions in Banach space theory.
method: They represent ideals as spaces c0(I) for I an ideal over natural numbers, and characterize the Grothendieck property using finitely additive measures.
result: They show that some analytic ideals yield Grothendieck spaces, while many Borel ideals do not, and that the Grothendieck property is not downward closed in the Katětov order.
conclusion: The work contributes to the theory of Banach lattices and ideals, but is unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: Construction Of Entropy Satisfying Active Flux-type Methods
authors: Yongle Liu Remi Abgrall
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper is devoted to the analysis of the entropy stability properties of Active Flux scheme for a hyperbolic system equipped with one entropy inequality. This type of scheme evolves two sets of degrees of freedom: point values that are chosen on the boundary of the elements that cover the computational domain, and the average of the solution in these elements. We show that the only thing to do is to get an entropy inequality for the average values, the point values degrees of freedom do not play any role. We construct a monolithic scheme which is bound preserving of , non oscillatory following , and entropy diminishing. The entropy condition is implemented in Tadmor's framework, i.e. for the semi-discrete scheme only. The scheme is tested on the Kurganov-Popov-Petrova test case which is known to sensitive to the satisfaction of an entropy inequality. We show that our entropy correction is effective: if we do not activate the bound-preserving nor the non oscillatory condition, we get the correct solution with some spurious wiggles, as expected. Though the development, implementation and tests are done with the triangle version of the scheme, the same method can be used for polygonal meshes, following .
tldr: This paper constructs entropy-stable Active Flux schemes for hyperbolic conservation laws, focusing on numerical methods rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To ensure entropy stability in Active Flux-type numerical schemes for hyperbolic systems, which is important for accurate simulations but unrelated to the user's research interests.
method: The authors derive an entropy inequality for the cell averages in a semi-discrete framework, and implement a monolithic scheme that is bound-preserving, non-oscillatory, and entropy-diminishing.
result: The entropy correction is effective on the Kurganov-Popov-Petrova test case, producing correct solutions even without bound-preserving or non-oscillatory conditions.
conclusion: The proposed method ensures entropy stability for Active Flux schemes and can be extended to polygonal meshes, but it is purely computational and not relevant to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: An Adaptive Phase Field Framework For Large-scale Interface Evolution Problems Using A Strong-form Gradient Smoothing Approach
authors: Zirui Mao, Alice Xu, Shenyang Hu, Panos Stinis, Yuyan Shao, Ang Li, Yulan Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiscale problems with evolving interfaces are ubiquitous in science and engineering. Phase-field models are a powerful tool for simulating interface-dominated phenomena in computational mechanics and materials modeling, but their application to large-scale problems is often constrained by the high computational cost of resolving thin diffuse interfaces over the entire domain. This paper presents an efficient strong-form phase-field solver that couples the Gradient Smoothing Method (GSM) with a hierarchical adaptive and moving structured mesh, enabling automatic localization of resolution within a narrow interfacial region while retaining coarse discretization in bulk domains. A layered refinement design is introduced to preserve locally uniform resolution across the interface, allowing the GSM discretization to maintain overall second-order accuracy despite strong mesh non-uniformity away from the interface. Although GSM incurs a higher per-degree-of-freedom cost than standard finite-difference schemes, the adaptive framework substantially reduces the total number of degrees of freedom, resulting in near-linear computational scaling compared with the quadratic scaling of uniform-grid approaches. Numerical examples based on the Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard equations demonstrate that the proposed adaptive GSM solver delivers desired accuracy for interface evolution while attaining more favorable computational complexity, O(N), than existing weak-form and strong-form solvers, becoming significantly more efficient for large-scale problems with thin interfaces or a small interfacial area fraction relative to the whole domain.
tldr: This paper presents an adaptive phase-field solver for large-scale interface evolution problems using a gradient smoothing method.
motivation: Phase-field models are computationally expensive for large-scale problems due to the need to resolve thin interfaces over the entire domain.
method: The authors couple the Gradient Smoothing Method (GSM) with a hierarchical adaptive and moving structured mesh, using a layered refinement design to maintain accuracy.
result: The adaptive framework achieves near-linear computational scaling O(N) compared to quadratic scaling of uniform-grid approaches, while maintaining second-order accuracy.
conclusion: The proposed solver is significantly more efficient for large-scale problems with thin interfaces or small interfacial area fraction.

title: Intercity Ev Charging Readiness In T\"urkiye: A Countrywide Scheduling And Economic Assessment
authors: Taner Cokyasar
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25143v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper assesses the readiness of T\"urkiye's electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure to support cost-competitive intercity travel compared to internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles. Utilizing a directed acyclic graph-based scheduling framework, charging stops are optimized for over 2 million synthetic intercity EV trips across the national highway network, evaluating 9,641 licensed charging stations. An eight-scenario case study examines the interplay between charger power (5--350 kW) and station capacity (5 and 50 plugs), supplemented by a 200-run parametric sensitivity analysis on EV range, discharge rate, charger power, and state-of-charge (SoC) operating bounds. A three-tier economic analysis isolates operational costs, total cost of ownership (TCO), and infrastructure investments. Economically, EVs demonstrate a 23--26% operational cost advantage driven by T\"urkiye's favorable fuel-to-electricity price ratio, maintaining a 10--12% TCO advantage despite higher purchase prices. However, full-system infrastructure savings heavily depend on station sizing, yielding positive returns at 5 plugs per station but negative returns at 50. Ultimately, vehicle discharge rate emerges as the dominant economic lever. This study provides the first countrywide, vehicle-level assessment of intercity EV charging readiness for an emerging market, offering actionable insights for policymakers on infrastructure gaps, station sizing tradeoffs, and adoption incentives.
tldr: This paper assesses the readiness of Turkey's EV charging infrastructure for intercity travel using a scheduling framework and economic analysis.
motivation: To evaluate whether EV intercity travel can be cost-competitive with ICE vehicles in an emerging market, and to provide policy insights.
method: A directed acyclic graph-based scheduling framework optimizes charging stops for over 2 million synthetic intercity EV trips across Turkey's highway network, considering 9,641 charging stations. An eight-scenario case study and 200-run parametric sensitivity analysis are performed.
result: EVs show a 23-26% operational cost advantage and 10-12% TCO advantage over ICE vehicles. Infrastructure savings depend on station sizing, with positive returns at 5 plugs per station but negative at 50. Vehicle discharge rate is the dominant economic lever.
conclusion: Turkey's EV charging infrastructure can support cost-competitive intercity travel, but station sizing and discharge rate are critical factors for economic viability.

title: A Foundational Perspective For Partitional Clustering On Networks
authors: Cem Iyigun Derya Ipek Eroglu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study presents a theoretical analysis of partitional clustering on networks, analyzing both hard and soft assignment schemes with different objective functions. Cluster centers are not restricted to vertices but can also be located along the edges. We examine four key models: P-Median (PMP) and Sum of Squares Clustering (SSC) under hard assignment, and Probabilistic Distance Clustering (PDC) and Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) under soft assignment. Through mathematical analysis, we uncover structural properties that differentiate these models, such as the significance of assignment bottleneck points and the role of vertex-restricted solutions in determining optimal cluster centers. Our findings reveal that, while SSC and FCM can yield optimal centers along edges, PMP and PDC inherently favor vertex placement, leading to insights into clustering behavior on networks. These insights offer new directions for designing efficient algorithms and have implications ranging from facility location and network design to clustering on the embedding graphs that power similarity search in modern retrieval systems.
tldr: This paper presents a theoretical analysis of partitional clustering on networks, comparing hard and soft assignment models with cluster centers possibly on edges.
motivation: To understand structural properties of clustering models on networks and their implications for algorithm design and applications like facility location.
method: Mathematical analysis of four clustering models (PMP, SSC, PDC, FCM) on networks, examining assignment bottleneck points and vertex-restricted solutions.
result: SSC and FCM can yield optimal centers along edges, while PMP and PDC favor vertex placement, revealing distinct clustering behaviors.
conclusion: These insights offer new directions for designing efficient clustering algorithms and have implications for network design and similarity search.

title: A Riemannian View On Active Subspaces
authors: Zachary Grey
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active subspaces provide an explainable, eigenvalue-ordered principle for studying how scalar-valued quantities of interest change the most, on average, over a reduced basis of Euclidean domains. Composition with parallel transport generalizes this principle from Euclidean space to quantities of interest defined over Riemannian manifolds, and the resulting intrinsic formulation is contrasted with the extrinsic, embedding-based gradient average of manifold learning. Either strategy is studied in an intrinsically local sense, restricted to mean-centered geodesic-balls, and within that scope the two are not identical: on the central tangent space, eigenvalues agree to second order in the geodesic radius of the sampled domain, while dominant eigenspaces agree at the same order relative to the spectral gap. Extending activity beyond that central space then calls for either recomputed decompositions over changing tangent spaces or, intrinsically, parallel transport of a single central frame. Hyperspheres are emphasized throughout as a particular manifold of interest, motivated by applications over preshape spaces for statistical shape analysis. Numerical examples over the 2-sphere illustrate the formalism, including the derived ridge recovery at a curvature-limited quadratic rate.
tldr: This paper extends active subspaces to Riemannian manifolds for dimension reduction in shape analysis.
motivation: Active subspaces are a tool for dimension reduction in Euclidean spaces, but many applications involve data on manifolds; the paper aims to generalize the concept to Riemannian manifolds.
method: The authors compose active subspaces with parallel transport to define intrinsic active subspaces on Riemannian manifolds, and compare with extrinsic embedding-based approaches. They analyze local behavior on geodesic balls and use hyperspheres as a key example.
result: Eigenvalues agree to second order in geodesic radius, and dominant eigenspaces agree at the same order relative to the spectral gap. Numerical examples on the 2-sphere demonstrate ridge recovery at a curvature-limited quadratic rate.
conclusion: The intrinsic formulation provides a principled way to perform active subspace analysis on manifolds, with potential applications in shape analysis and other fields.

title: A Convex Splitting Spectral Method For The Phase Field Crystal Equation: Energy Stability, Computational Stability Maps, And Three-Dimensional Gpu Simulations
authors: Saulo Orizaga, Peimeng Yin, Deep Choudhuri
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an efficient Fourier spectral method based on the convex splitting framework of Eyre~ for the phase field crystal (PFC) equation. The proposed first-order scheme is unconditionally energy stable and conserves mass to machine precision. An energy stability theorem is established using a truncated potential argument, and a semi-analytical neutral stability curve is derived from a dominant-mode energy balance, providing a closed-form characterization of the practical stability boundary. The classical sufficient condition [MATH] is shown to be conservative: a computational stability map obtained from 40,000 GPU-accelerated PFC simulations reveals that energy-stable solutions persist for values of [MATH] significantly below this threshold. Crucially, accuracy analysis demonstrates that smaller values of [MATH] within the stable region consistently yield lower [MATH] errors. This high-fidelity regime is rigorously verified through an extended asymptotic stress test consisting of a long-time three-dimensional simulation on a [MATH] grid up to [MATH], successfully executing [MATH] continuous temporal increments deep within the relaxed stability regime, well below the classical convex splitting limit ([MATH]), while preserving strict monotonic energy dissipation and machine-precision mass conservation. Finally, two-dimensional and three-dimensional simulations at resolutions up to [MATH] are performed on a single consumer GPU, demonstrating the scalability of the proposed framework for resolving complex phase-field dynamics without requiring HPC infrastructure. The code is made publicly available on GitHub.
tldr: This paper presents a numerical method for the phase field crystal equation, focusing on computational stability and GPU simulations.
motivation: To develop an efficient and stable numerical scheme for simulating phase field crystal dynamics, which is important for materials science.
method: A convex splitting Fourier spectral method is used, with energy stability analysis and computational stability maps derived from GPU-accelerated simulations.
result: The method achieves unconditional energy stability and mass conservation, and reveals that the classical stability condition is conservative, allowing larger time steps.
conclusion: The proposed method is scalable and accurate for large-scale 3D simulations on consumer GPUs, enabling high-fidelity phase-field dynamics without HPC infrastructure.

title: Parallelisation Of Discrete Exterior Calculus Via Representation Theory On Curved And Three-Dimensional Meshes
authors: Leon D. Da Silva, Marcelo P. Santos, Jos\'e D. Da Silva, Gilson Ferreira Jr
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a universal block-diagonalization framework for Discrete Exterior Calculus (DEC) operators on symmetric meshes, enabling embarrassingly parallel solvers with provable FLOP reductions. We prove that the two fundamental DEC operators, the discrete exterior derivative [MATH] and the Hodge star [MATH], are equivariant under isometric finite group actions on simplicial complexes. The proof exploits the permutation representation induced on cochain spaces by the group action. As a consequence, any operator assembled from [MATH] and [MATH] (including the Hodge Laplacian, the codifferential, Maxwell-type operators, and elasticity operators) inherits a block-diagonal structure in a single symmetry-adapted basis, which is computed only once per mesh. Unlike spectral methods restricted to flat Platonic domains, the framework applies natively to curved manifolds and is applicable in principle to computational electromagnetism and geometric fluid simulation on symmetric domains. Numerical experiments on a geodesic sphere ([MATH] symmetry) and a hexagonal torus ([MATH] symmetry) yield FLOP-based parallel speedups, relative to a dense direct factorization, of up to [MATH] and [MATH], respectively. A further experiment on a body-centred-cubic (BCC) tessellation of the flat 3-torus [MATH] with [MATH] symmetry confirms equivariance of the exterior derivative, Hodge star, and Hodge Laplacian at machine precision for form degrees [MATH] across three mesh resolutions. The FLOP-based sequential speedup approaches its theoretical asymptote of [MATH], which a standard Schur-multiplicity reduction deepens by a further factor of order [MATH]. These results show that a single symmetry-adapted basis reduces the linear-solve cost of structure-preserving DEC computations on curved and three-dimensional meshes.
tldr: This paper presents a block-diagonalization framework for Discrete Exterior Calculus operators on symmetric meshes, enabling parallel solvers for computational electromagnetism and fluid simulation.
motivation: To accelerate structure-preserving numerical methods on curved and 3D meshes by exploiting symmetry to reduce computational cost.
method: Proves equivariance of DEC operators under isometric finite group actions and constructs a symmetry-adapted basis that block-diagonalizes the operators.
result: Achieves FLOP-based speedups up to 100x on geodesic sphere and hexagonal torus, and confirms equivariance at machine precision on a BCC 3-torus.
conclusion: The symmetry-adapted basis provides significant computational savings for DEC computations on symmetric domains, applicable to electromagnetism and fluid dynamics.

title: Distributed Nonlinear Equality-Constrained Optimization Via Feedback Linearization And Singular Perturbation
authors: Zihao Ren, Lei Wang, Hongye Su, Guodong Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed optimization becomes particularly challenging when nonconvex objectives are combined with nonlinear equality constraints: feasibility is network coupled, while most existing exponentially convergent methods rely on convexity or affine constraints. This paper introduces a feedback-linearization and singular-perturbation framework for two representative problem classes involving, respectively, distributed local nonlinear equality constraints and nonlinear aggregate equality constraints. The framework separates the regulation of consensus and feasibility residuals from optimization along the feasible manifold. Specifically, an ideal feedback-linearized dynamics is constructed whose output behavior can be explicitly assigned, while its zero-output dynamics coincides with the projected gradient flow of the aggregate objective on the feasible manifold. The ideal feedback-linearizing input, however, is determined by a state-dependent, network-coupled algebraic equation and is therefore not directly implementable in a distributed manner. To overcome this obstruction, we replace the nonlocal algebraic solution with a fast residual-tracking dynamics, yielding a singular-perturbation realization that uses only local and neighboring information. Under a local quadratic-growth condition imposed only on the feasible manifold, we establish local exponential convergence of both the ideal and distributed dynamics. For sufficiently strong time-scale separation, the convergence rate of the distributed realization can be chosen arbitrarily close to that of the ideal dynamics. Explicit Euler discretizations are also proved to preserve local exponential convergence. Under stronger manifold regularity conditions, the region of attraction extends to a tubular neighborhood of the feasible manifold and, for affine local equality constraints, to the whole admissible state space.
tldr: This paper proposes a distributed optimization framework for nonconvex objectives with nonlinear equality constraints using feedback linearization and singular perturbation.
motivation: Distributed optimization with nonconvex objectives and nonlinear equality constraints is challenging because feasibility is network-coupled and existing methods rely on convexity or affine constraints.
method: The framework separates consensus/feasibility regulation from optimization via an ideal feedback-linearized dynamics, then replaces the nonlocal algebraic solution with a fast residual-tracking dynamics using singular perturbation.
result: Local exponential convergence is established for both ideal and distributed dynamics under a local quadratic-growth condition, with rates arbitrarily close to ideal under strong time-scale separation.
conclusion: The approach provides a distributed solution for nonlinear equality-constrained optimization with provable convergence, extending to affine constraints globally.

title: Projection And Contraction Methods With Double Inertial Steps For Variational Inclusion Problems On Hilbert Spaces
authors: Moin Uddin, Mohammed Alshahrani, Qamrul Hasan Ansari
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose three projection--contraction algorithms for solving variational inclusion problems in the setting of Hilbert spaces, each incorporating a double inertial technique into the projection--contraction framework. The first algorithm \algoO achieves weak convergence under monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity of the single-valued operator, with an adaptive stepsize rule that does not require prior knowledge of the Lipschitz constant. A modified variant \algoT of \algoO attains [MATH]-linear convergence under the strong monotonicity assumption. The third algorithm \algoDIM obtains strong convergence to the minimum-norm solution without requiring strong monotonicity. We illustrate the proposed methods on an abstract variational inclusion problem and apply them to the split feasibility problem and the elastic net regularization problem, comparing them with existing methods in the literature. The [MATH]-linear convergence of \algoT is also verified through numerical simulations.
tldr: This paper proposes projection-contraction algorithms with double inertial steps for solving variational inclusion problems in Hilbert spaces.
motivation: To develop efficient numerical methods for variational inclusion problems, which are important in optimization and applied mathematics.
method: Three projection-contraction algorithms are introduced, each incorporating a double inertial technique; convergence is analyzed under monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity assumptions.
result: Weak convergence is achieved for the first algorithm, linear convergence for a modified variant under strong monotonicity, and strong convergence to the minimum-norm solution for the third algorithm.
conclusion: The proposed methods are effective for variational inclusion problems and are demonstrated on split feasibility and elastic net regularization problems.

title: Event-Triggered Discrete-Time Multivariable Extremum Seeking Systems
authors: Victor Hugo Pereira Rodrigues, Tiago Roux Oliveira, Miroslav Krsti\'c, Frank Allg\"ower
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a discrete-time event-triggered extremum seeking framework for real-time optimization of multivariable nonlinear systems. In contrast to conventional discrete-time extremum seeking implementations that rely on periodic input updates, the proposed scheme updates the control action only when a state-dependent triggering condition is met, enabling aperiodic execution and substantial reduction of actuation and communication effort. The resulting closed-loop architecture reconciles two structurally different paradigms: the periodic excitation required for gradient recovery in extremum seeking and the aperiodic philosophy of event-triggered control. By combining discrete-time averaging arguments with Lyapunov-based analysis, we prove practical convergence of the system trajectories to a neighborhood of the unknown extremum and exponential stability of the corresponding average dynamics despite the loss of uniform sampling.
