Rather than relying on the CWE->CAPEC->ATT&CK derivation chain, whose table-expansion artifacts we quantify, we train a multi-label classifier on a curated gold dataset of 1,207 CVEs from expert MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense mappings. The resulting model approximately doubles recall@5 compared with a zero-shot embedding-similarity baseline and improves every ranking metric. We then investigate whether LLM-assisted labeling can extend the gold dataset. Initial experiments suggest contradictory conclusions: a single run indicates degraded performance, while averaging over five random seeds suggests a small gain. However, an independent replication and an expansion-size study (100--984 additional CVEs) show that the apparent improvement is an evaluation artifact. LLM-generated labels, with approximately 0.39 agreement with expert annotations, provide no reliable improvement at any expansion size and reduce rare-technique coverage at around 1,000 added CVEs (macro-F1 decreases by 0.04). The root cause is evaluation noise. Selecting checkpoints on a small test split effectively maximizes over many noisy evaluations, producing recall@5 differences of up to 0.05 between otherwise identical runs. Using a corrected protocol based on validation-split checkpoint selection, the gold-only model achieves recall@5 of (0.673 \pm 0.019), and repeating the decisive experiment confirms the null result for LLM expansion. A final scaling study shows that additional expert-curated data consistently improves performance, whereas LLM-labeled data does not, indicating that the classifier is limited by label quality rather than dataset size. All datasets, models, code, and training logs are publicly released.
tldr: This paper presents a pipeline for mapping CVEs to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, focusing on cybersecurity threat intelligence, not quantum information theory.
motivation: The authors aim to improve the mapping of vulnerability descriptions to attack techniques, addressing limitations of existing derivation chains and evaluating the utility of LLM-assisted labeling.
method: They train a multi-label classifier on a curated gold dataset of 1,207 CVEs and test LLM-assisted label expansion, using validation-split checkpoint selection to avoid evaluation noise.
result: The gold-only model achieves recall@5 of 0.673, while LLM-generated labels provide no reliable improvement and reduce rare-technique coverage.
conclusion: Additional expert-curated data improves performance, but LLM-labeled data does not, indicating label quality is the limiting factor.

title: Kernel-Checked Exclusions For The Erd\H{o}s-Selfridge Odd Covering Problem: Any Odd Covering Of $\mathbb{Z}$ Has Lcm Exceeding 10000
authors: Shayaan Siddique Ibrahim Mian
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Erds-Selfridge odd covering problem (Erds problem #7) asks whether a covering system of [MATH] exists whose moduli are all odd, distinct, and greater than 1. The problem is open. We present a Lean 4 formalization, checked end to end by the proof kernel, of the exclusion: any covering of [MATH] by finitely many congruence classes with distinct odd moduli > 1 has lcm of the moduli exceeding 10000. The proof composes a formalized density argument (a covering by divisors of [MATH] exceeding 1 forces [MATH], so the lcm is abundant or perfect), a kernel-checked abundancy floor (no odd [MATH] qualifies), a family of Chinese-Remainder capacity certificates -- decidable per-[MATH] arithmetic inequalities each refuting every covering with distinct moduli > 1 dividing that [MATH] -- for all 23 odd abundant numbers below [MATH], and a kernel-checked enumeration establishing that those 23 are the only odd non-deficient candidates. The result is transported to the official StrictCoveringSystem [MATH] formulation of Erds #7 in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, with a bidirectional periodicity bridge between coverings of [MATH] and finite checks over [MATH] suitable for consuming future SAT-style search output. All 63 published theorems depend on exactly propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound: no sorry, no native_decide, no solver in the trusted base. The mathematical content is known -- the density argument is folklore, and far larger uncertified classifications of covering numbers exist -- so the contribution is epistemic rather than mathematical: these exclusions are theorems of the Lean kernel, with an axiom gate enforced mechanically in continuous integration.
tldr: This paper formalizes a known mathematical exclusion for the Erdős–Selfridge odd covering problem using the Lean 4 proof assistant, but does not contribute to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The Erdős–Selfridge odd covering problem is a long-standing open problem in number theory; the authors aim to provide a fully kernel-checked proof that any odd covering of integers must have lcm exceeding 10000.
method: The proof uses a density argument, abundancy floor checks, Chinese-Remainder capacity certificates for 23 odd abundant numbers, and a bidirectional periodicity bridge, all formalized in Lean 4 with minimal axioms.
result: The formalization proves that any covering of ℤ by finitely many congruence classes with distinct odd moduli >1 has lcm > 10000, and the proof is verified by the Lean kernel.
conclusion: The contribution is epistemic (formal verification) rather than mathematical, and has no connection to the user's research interests in quantum information theory.

title: Universal Individual-Sequence Prediction With A Primitive-Recursive Superpredictor
authors: Amir Leshem
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study sequential prediction of individual binary sequences under zero-one loss. No computable master can compete on every sequence with all total computable predictors. We therefore consider rational-valued primitive-recursive forecasters, a broad syntactically enumerable class containing finite-state, context-based, and Prediction by Partial Matching (PPM) rules. We construct a computable probabilistic predictor with an explicit sublinear regret bound relative to every primitive-recursive forecaster on every individual sequence. We further prove that the PPM predictor is primitive recursive. Consequently, our predictor attains the infinite-past Bayes error on every Martin-L\"of random realization of every computable stationary ergodic binary source. This optimality extends to finitely many independent such sources interleaved according to an arbitrary primitive-recursive schedule. Finally, we establish strict separations from finite-state prediction and from every fixed primitive-recursive predictor. keywords: Universal prediction, individual sequences, prediction with expert advice, primitive recursive functions, Kolmogorov complexity, PPM.
tldr: This paper studies universal sequential prediction of individual binary sequences using primitive-recursive forecasters, achieving sublinear regret bounds.
motivation: To construct a computable predictor that can compete with all primitive-recursive forecasters on every individual sequence, addressing limitations of computable masters.
method: The paper constructs a probabilistic predictor with explicit sublinear regret bounds relative to any primitive-recursive forecaster, and proves that the PPM predictor is primitive recursive.
result: The predictor attains the infinite-past Bayes error on every Martin-Löf random realization of any computable stationary ergodic binary source, and extends to interleaved sources.
conclusion: The work establishes strict separations from finite-state prediction and fixed primitive-recursive predictors, demonstrating the power of primitive-recursive forecasters.

title: Algorithms For Candidate Control In Greedy Participatory Budgeting Rules
authors: Krzysztof Sornat \v{s}imon Schierreich
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of candidate control in participatory budgeting elections. Our focus is on two prominent sequential welfare-based rules---GreedyAV and GreedyCost---which are widely used in practice. Candidate control asks whether we can strategically modify the set of available candidates so as to either ensure that a preferred candidate [MATH] is selected or prevent [MATH] from being selected. Since all variants of candidate control under the two rules we consider are known to be NP-hard, we analyze the problems through the lens of parameterized complexity and approximability. Under the first lens, we provide a comprehensive classification with respect to natural parameters such as the number of voters, the number of controlled candidates, and the number of distinct costs, as well as their combinations. Within the second perspective, we establish a tight approximability bound.
tldr: This paper studies candidate control in participatory budgeting elections using greedy welfare-based rules.
motivation: To understand the computational complexity of strategic candidate manipulation in participatory budgeting.
method: Parameterized complexity analysis and approximability bounds for candidate control problems under GreedyAV and GreedyCost rules.
result: Comprehensive classification of parameterized complexity and tight approximability bounds for the problems.
conclusion: The problems remain hard under various parameterizations, but some fixed-parameter tractable cases exist.

title: A Structuration Approach To Theorizing Cybersecurity Practice: The Starc Model
authors: Md Aktaruzzaman, Atif Ahmad, Sean Maynard
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The problem: Cybersecurity practice runs simultaneously across analysts, teams, organizations, sectors, and regulators, co-evolves with adversaries, and increasingly blends human and algorithmic decision-making. The theories applied to it operate at single organizational levels and cannot explain why organizations with broadly similar controls differ sharply in resilience. This paper: We develop STARC (Structuration Theory Adaptation for Resilient Cybersecurity), a framework for locating where cybersecurity practice succeeds or fails structurally. It extends Giddens' Structuration Theory with three innovations, Multi-Level Adversarial Agency, Threat-Adaptive Structuration, and Material-Agential Structural Properties, across five structure-agency triads. Evidence base: STARC is illustrated through re-analysis of three financial organizations, an Australian, an Indonesian, and a Malaysian bank, across 20 interviews from SOC analysts to senior executives, selected as diverse insourced and outsourced configurations rather than as a comparison of equivalents. Cybersecurity contribution: STARC offers a structural account of why differently resourced and outsourced organizations differ in resilience, and a vocabulary for diagnosing incident-response breakdown across levels, tempos, and the human-algorithm authority boundary that single-level frameworks leave invisible. Theory and outputs: It extends Structuration Theory to adversarial, multi-level, and hybrid human-algorithmic contexts, and yields seven testable propositions linking structuration to resilience, offered for future testing.
tldr: This paper develops a structuration theory framework for cybersecurity practice, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Existing cybersecurity theories operate at single organizational levels and fail to explain differences in resilience across organizations.
method: The authors extend Giddens' Structuration Theory with three innovations and illustrate the framework through re-analysis of interviews from three banks.
result: The STARC framework provides a structural account of resilience differences and yields seven testable propositions.
conclusion: STARC offers a vocabulary for diagnosing incident-response breakdowns across levels and human-algorithm boundaries.

title: Verification Of Provers And Solvers
authors: Ren\'e Thiemann
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic deduction tools such as automatic theorem provers, SAT (satisfiability) solvers, SMT (satisfiability modulo theories) solvers, and termination analyzers can be connected to proof assistants using various approaches, notably by certification and verification. This chapter reviews and compares the approaches available, and mentions several successful applications.
tldr: This paper reviews approaches for connecting automatic deduction tools to proof assistants via certification and verification.
motivation: To compare and contrast certification and verification methods for integrating automatic theorem provers, SAT/SMT solvers, and termination analyzers with proof assistants.
method: The chapter reviews existing approaches, categorizing them into certification and verification, and discusses several successful applications.
result: The paper provides a comparative analysis of the two approaches, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses.
conclusion: Certification and verification are both viable strategies, with the choice depending on the specific tool and proof assistant context.

title: From Role Prompt To Infinite Thinking: Exploiting Persona Conditioning For Inference Cost Attacks In LLMs
authors: Zhiyi Mou, Wangze Ni, Tianfang Xiao, Haoyang LI, Chen Jason Zhang, Hanzhi Ma, Yang Bai, Zhibo Wang, Kui Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, making inference efficiency and service reliability critical concerns due to their substantial computational costs. However, the autoregressive generation mechanism of LLMs enables malicious prompts to manipulate generation behaviors, inducing excessive token generation that amplifies computational consumption and threatens service efficiency. Existing methods mainly rely on adversarial suffixes or explicit extension instructions, which introduce detectable behaviors and limit their applicability. In this paper, we reveal a previously unexplored vulnerability caused by persona consistency in LLMs, where models maintain assigned roles and reproduce corresponding behaviors even when they result in inefficient reasoning and excessive generation. Based on this observation, we propose RolePlay, a task-aware dynamic persona alignment framework that constructs adaptive personas to naturally induce inefficient yet semantically coherent behaviors for inference cost amplification. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and diverse task datasets demonstrate that RolePlay consistently outperforms existing inference extension methods, achieving an average token amplification of up to and a maximum token amplification ratio of . Our findings identify persona conditioning as a new attack surface for LLM inference efficiency and offer a new perspective on computational cost amplification.
tldr: This paper identifies a vulnerability in LLMs where persona conditioning can be exploited to induce excessive token generation, increasing inference costs.
motivation: LLM inference is computationally expensive, and existing attack methods are detectable; the authors aim to reveal a new attack surface via persona consistency.
method: They propose RolePlay, a task-aware dynamic persona alignment framework that constructs adaptive personas to naturally induce inefficient yet coherent generation.
result: RolePlay achieves significant token amplification, outperforming existing inference extension methods across multiple LLMs and tasks.
conclusion: Persona conditioning is a new attack surface for LLM inference efficiency, highlighting the need for defenses against such computational cost amplification attacks.

title: Effort Matters In Score-Based Admissions: How Retaking And Aggregation Shape Test Scores
authors: Christine Ling, Diptangshu Sen, Juba Ziani
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observed standardized test scores are the result of an endogenous process: students strategically allocate effort across multiple retake attempts to improve their outcomes. Because students differ in their ability to make these investments, the interaction between applicant strategy and institutional scoring rules---such as the widely used Single-Sitting and Superscoring policies---can disparately distort observed scores. We develop a strategic framework where students allocate effort in response to different scoring policies. We show that Superscoring---the practice of combining the best section scores across attempts---introduces systematic score inflation through order-statistic selection over noise draws. This degrades signal accuracy and amplifies wealth-based disparities by disproportionately rewarding applicants who can afford repeated testing. Conversely, Single-Sitting---which keeps the best overall score rather than section-level scores---preserves signal fidelity but excludes high-ability students who lack the resources to prepare for all subjects simultaneously. Neither rule uniformly dominates; instead, they force a structural trade-off between statistical precision and fair outcomes. Finally, to address this, we propose three algorithmic interventions which either modify how scores from multiple attempts are combined, or apply a post-hoc correction to observed scores. Using simulations calibrated to 2025 College Board data, we compare standard scoring rules against these proposed interventions.
tldr: This paper studies how retaking and aggregation policies in standardized testing affect score inflation and fairness, with no connection to quantum information theory.
motivation: The paper addresses fairness and accuracy in score-based admissions, but the topic is entirely outside quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors develop a strategic framework where students allocate effort across retakes, and compare scoring policies like Superscoring and Single-Sitting using simulations calibrated to College Board data.
result: Superscoring inflates scores and amplifies wealth-based disparities, while Single-Sitting preserves signal fidelity but may exclude high-ability students lacking resources.
conclusion: Neither policy dominates; the paper proposes algorithmic interventions to balance precision and fairness, but this is unrelated to quantum information research.

title: \textsc{IH-Benchmark}: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark For Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness In Llm Applications
authors: Conor Mccauley, Zeliang Kan, Jason Martin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. Existing benchmarks answer this only partially, often focusing on a single hierarchy edge or adapting public datasets with limited tool-use coverage. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct system-user conflicts (S>U) and tool-mediated user-tool (U>T) conflicts. IH-Benchmark is built from a human-authored taxonomy of 44 constraint families across generic, health, finance, retail, and coding settings, and evaluates scenarios with a uniform binary pass/fail protocol combining a predicate DSL with category-scoped LLM judges. Across 37 evaluated models, hierarchy compliance ranges from 98.2% to 20.5%. We find that strong S>U compliance is not a reliable proxy for U>T robustness: several models preserve system constraints under direct user conflict but degrade sharply when conflicting instructions appear in tool outputs. Constraint hardening also reveals a split between models: some failures are largely fixed by stronger warnings, while others persist across all strictness levels. Finally, the most revealing failures are often subtle rather than overtly dangerous; models resist unauthorized purchases or bulk ticket closure more reliably than injected disclaimers or small factual distortions. These results suggest that instruction-hierarchy robustness is not a single capability, but a set of behaviors that must be evaluated across conflict surfaces, constraint types, and attack presentations.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating instruction-hierarchy robustness in LLMs, focusing on conflicts between system, user, and tool instructions.
motivation: Existing benchmarks for instruction hierarchy robustness are limited, often covering only single conflict types or lacking tool-use scenarios.
method: The authors construct a taxonomy of 44 constraint families across multiple domains and evaluate models using a binary pass/fail protocol with predicate DSL and LLM judges.
result: Evaluation of 37 models shows compliance ranging from 98.2% to 20.5%, revealing that system-user compliance does not predict user-tool robustness and that some failures persist despite stronger warnings.
conclusion: Instruction-hierarchy robustness is a multifaceted capability requiring evaluation across different conflict surfaces and constraint types.

title: Does Runtime Topology Context Improve LLM-Generated Kubernetes Security Patches?
authors: Farooq Shaikh
abstract: ArXiv:2607.25995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kubernetes is central to the cloud-native ecosystem, orchestrating containerised workloads. Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can automate cluster security remediation, generating configuration patches from Kubernetes Security Posture Management (KSPM) findings without human authoring. Such systems, however, prompt the model with each finding in isolation from the live service call graph, assuming general hardening knowledge suffices. This assumption breaks down whenever a patch must preserve a runtime service dependency invisible to the model: an otherwise compliant fix then carries a destructive functional blast radius, crashing downstream callers or silently severing call edges across the cluster. Whether live cluster context improves patch correctness has not been measured under controlled conditions across multiple dependency classes. We introduce KuTIE (Kubernetes Topology Intelligence Engine), which builds a live cluster context from Istio call edges, Trivy KSPM findings, and the service-account bindings a workload reads, and conditions LLM patch generation on it. It is evaluated on VulnCare, a purpose-built 36-deployment, four-namespace healthcare cluster with 31 injectable findings across seven dependency classes, each labelled by topology dependence against cluster ground truth. Across 248 trials, topology context raises topology-dependent patch correctness from 11.1% to 78.0% ([MATH]), a gap that holds for every model and for six of seven classes, from credential and network-policy ([MATH]) to role-based access control ([MATH]); a topology-independent control exhibits no such effect ([MATH]), isolating the result from generic prompt enrichment. Supplying the live service-call graph and the service-account bindings it exposes thus improves remediation of topology-dependent findings well beyond scanner-only context.
tldr: This paper investigates whether providing live cluster topology context improves LLM-generated Kubernetes security patches.
motivation: Current LLM-based patch generation for Kubernetes security findings ignores runtime service dependencies, leading to patches that break cluster functionality.
method: The authors introduce KuTIE, which enriches LLM prompts with live Istio call edges, Trivy KSPM findings, and service-account bindings, and evaluate it on a purpose-built healthcare cluster with 31 findings across seven dependency classes.
result: Topology context raises topology-dependent patch correctness from 11.1% to 78.0%, with consistent improvement across models and dependency classes.
conclusion: Supplying live service-call graph and service-account bindings significantly improves remediation of topology-dependent findings beyond scanner-only context.

title: Proportional Fairness For Harmful Decisions
authors: Benjamin Cookson, Soroush Ebadian, Dominik Peters, Nisarg Shah
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study allocation of (divisible) public bads, where agents incur costs for alternatives and the goal is to pick a lottery over the alternatives. We show that the traditional definitions of the core, a central criterion of proportional representation for allocation of public goods, private goods, and private bads (chores), do not make sense for allocation of public bads. We introduce two formalizations of the core tailored to public bads. Under a structural condition which subsumes allocation of private bads, we show that zero-respecting Lindahl equilibria satisfy both formalizations, exhibit additional fairness guarantees, and strictly generalize competitive equilibria from equal incomes (CEEI) for allocation of private bads. Without this structural condition, we show that Lindahl equilibria exhibit undesirable behaviors, prove sharp impossibility results separating public bads from public goods, but show that a rule using a reduction to public goods recovers one of our formalizations of the core. Our results lay the groundwork for studying fair allocation of public bads, an overlooked yet fundamental problem, and highlight several structural and algorithmic directions that remain open.
tldr: This paper studies fair allocation of public bads using concepts from cooperative game theory and welfare economics, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The problem of fairly allocating harmful public goods (public bads) is overlooked in the fair division literature, and traditional core definitions fail for public bads.
method: The authors introduce two new core formalizations for public bads, analyze Lindahl equilibria under a structural condition, and prove impossibility results without it.
result: Zero-respecting Lindahl equilibria satisfy both core formalizations under a structural condition and generalize CEEI for private bads; without the condition, Lindahl equilibria exhibit undesirable behaviors.
conclusion: The work lays groundwork for fair allocation of public bads, highlighting structural and algorithmic open problems.

title: Freely Generated $n$-categories, Coinserters And Presentations Of Low Dimensional Categories
authors: Fernando Lucatelli Nunes
abstract: ArXiv:1704.04474v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A presentation records not only a categorical structure but also how it is assembled. This matters for rewriting, coherence, and minimality: freely adjoining a cell with prescribed boundary is different from imposing an equation between cells already constructed. We show that these two operations are governed, respectively, by coinserters and coequifiers, giving a uniform account of computadic presentations from ordinary categories to strict higher categories. For a graph [MATH], the free category on [MATH] is the coinserter in [MATH] of its domain and codomain maps between discrete categories. More generally, for every [MATH], freely adjoining [MATH]-cells with prescribed parallel boundaries to a strict [MATH]-category is a coinserter in the [MATH]-category of strict [MATH]-categories, strict [MATH]-functors, and [MATH]-icons. This construction is left adjoint to the underlying derivation-scheme functor. It recovers free strict [MATH]-categories from computads, while coequifiers impose equations between freely generated cells. In dimension two, it also satisfies a bicategorical universal property for normal pseudofunctors and icons. Replacing the walking arrow by the unit interval yields the topological coinserter of a graph. For a groupoidal [MATH]-computad [MATH], attaching one disk for each relation produces a presentation complex [MATH] whose fundamental groupoid is the groupoid presented by [MATH]. Consequently, the rank-finite deficiency of a connected groupoid is the classical deficiency of any isotropy group. Homology gives a sharp lower bound on the relations required to present a thin groupoid over a fixed graph, while crossed modules extend the comparison to relations among relations. Finally, for the descent computad, the identity and associativity confluences form a homotopy basis and attain the corresponding homological lower bounds.
tldr: This paper develops a categorical framework for freely adjoining cells and imposing equations in strict higher categories using coinserters and coequifiers.
motivation: To provide a uniform account of presentations for higher categories, clarifying the difference between freely adjoining a cell and imposing an equation.
method: Uses 2-categorical universal constructions (coinserters and coequifiers) in the category of strict n-categories, and relates them to computads and topological constructions.
result: Shows that freely adjoining n-cells is a coinserter, and coequifiers impose equations; recovers free strict n-categories from computads and gives homological bounds for groupoid presentations.
conclusion: The work offers a systematic approach to presentations of higher categories, with applications to rewriting, coherence, and homotopy theory.

title: Backpropagation For Effectful Languages I: Finite Probability And Discrete Output Algebraic Effects
authors: Diogo Simm, Fernando Lucatelli Nunes, Matthijs V\'ak\'ar
abstract: ArXiv:2607.13935v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We analyse reverse-mode automatic differentiation (AD) for discrete probabilistic programs. Our construction is formulated in the framework of Combinatory Homomorphic Automatic Differentiation (CHAD), treating AD as a structure-preserving transformation of programs, guided by a denotational semantics. The main case study is the finite atomic distribution monad, whose computations have finite support and differentiable weights. The key point is that differentiating probabilistic programs requires cotangents to flow backwards not only through deterministic computations, but also through the probabilistic structure itself. We define the corresponding reverse-mode code transformation and prove its correctness, for handled real-output programs, by a categorical logical-relations argument. Although the paper focuses on finite discrete probability, the construction gives a reusable pattern for differentiating discrete-output algebraic effects, including finite multiset non-determinism (e.g., from fork-join parallelism), exceptions, and writer-style accumulation (e.g., for in-place accumulation of high-dimensional vectors). More broadly, we view this work as a foundational step towards extending CHAD to richer probabilistic languages and to other algebraic effects with handlers.
tldr: This paper presents a reverse-mode automatic differentiation method for discrete probabilistic programs using the CHAD framework, focusing on finite probability and algebraic effects.
motivation: To enable gradient-based learning in probabilistic programming languages with discrete distributions, which require differentiation through probabilistic structures.
method: The authors extend Combinatory Homomorphic Automatic Differentiation (CHAD) to handle the finite atomic distribution monad and other discrete-output algebraic effects, using categorical logical-relations to prove correctness.
result: They define a correct reverse-mode code transformation for discrete probabilistic programs with differentiable weights, and show the pattern generalizes to other effects like nondeterminism and exceptions.
conclusion: This work provides a foundational step for extending automatic differentiation to richer probabilistic languages and algebraic effects, but is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: PATHFinder Agent For Tailored Prenatal Care
authors: Vaibhav Balloli, Carissa Samuel, Samia Abdelnabi, Alex Peahl, Elizabeth Bondi-Kelly
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24768v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Prenatal care is an important preventive service designed to improve outcomes for pregnant individuals. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recently introduced guidelines advocating tailored prenatal care, called PATH (Plan for Tailored Healthcare). We present PATHFinder Agent(Planner for Appropriate Tailored Healthcare), an end-to-end conversational agentic system that gathers patient health and social context through structured dialogue, curates individualized prenatal care plans aligned with PATH guidelines, and surfaces community resources from Michigan 211. The system features a four-stage workflow spanning patient intake, dynamic interaction, plan synthesis, and clinician oversight. We evaluate frontier large language models (LLMs) on expert-curated rubrics across five clinical dimensions, finding that GPT-5.2 achieves the highest average score (77.6\%) while identifying key gaps in antenatal testing recommendations. We discuss future validation through human participant studies and randomized controlled trials.
tldr: This paper presents an AI agent for personalized prenatal care planning based on ACOG guidelines.
motivation: To implement tailored prenatal care as recommended by new ACOG guidelines using an automated conversational agent.
method: The system uses a four-stage workflow with LLMs to gather patient context, generate care plans, and surface community resources.
result: GPT-5.2 achieved the highest average score (77.6%) on expert-curated rubrics, but gaps in antenatal testing recommendations were identified.
conclusion: The PATHFinder agent shows promise for automating prenatal care planning, but further validation through human studies is needed.

title: Stronger Memory-Query Tradeoffs For Convex Optimization: The Limitations Of Subquadratic Memory
authors: Michael Menart, Aleksandar Nikolov, Ohad Shamir
abstract: ArXiv:2607.24827v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove two lower bounds for the first order oracle complexity of minimizing a [MATH]-dimensional [MATH]-Lipschitz convex function over the unit ball with [MATH] bits of memory. We first show that any such (possibly randomized) algorithm must make [MATH] oracle queries. For deterministic optimization algorithms, we show that [MATH] queries are required. For all memory regimes of interest, these improves upon the previous best known lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for randomized and deterministic algorithms respectively. Notably, due to existing upper bounds, our lower bound for deterministic algorithms is the first to show a sharp oracle complexity phase transition around [MATH], where a polylogarithmic change in memory leads to a [MATH] change in the number of required oracle calls. Further, when the suboptimality is polynomially small in [MATH], our lower bound randomized algorithms is the first to show that [MATH] memory is necessary to nearly match the optimal query complexity among algorithms without memory constraints. Previously, such a result was only known for the regime where the suboptimality is quasipolynomially small in [MATH].
tldr: This paper proves lower bounds on the number of oracle queries required for convex optimization under memory constraints.
motivation: Understanding the fundamental tradeoffs between memory and query complexity in convex optimization is important for algorithm design.
method: The authors use information-theoretic arguments and adversarial constructions to derive lower bounds for both randomized and deterministic algorithms.
result: They show that any randomized algorithm requires Ω(n^2) queries and any deterministic algorithm requires Ω(n^2 log n) queries when memory is sublinear.
conclusion: The results reveal sharp phase transitions in oracle complexity as a function of memory, showing that subquadratic memory cannot achieve optimal query complexity.
